title: design: external OAuth 2.0 / OIDC provider — third-party app integration via standard authorization-code flow
description:
## Why now

Cloudflare's 2026-06 "OAuth for All" announcement (https://blog.cloudflare.com/oauth-for-all/) opened OAuth delegation to any Worker — every developer on CF can now ship an OAuth-server surface. That raises a substrate-trust question for ART: should notme expose a CF-compatible OAuth dance so third-party apps that already speak OAuth (and may be deployed on CF) can use notme as their identity provider, the way they'd OAuth into Google / GitHub today?

## What's already shipped vs missing

notme's identity-bridge surface (per cloister.capnp `wellKnownIdentityBridge` route kind) already ships: `/.well-known/openid-configuration`, `/.well-known/jwks.json`, `/.well-known/webfinger`, `/.well-known/nostr.json`, `POST /oauth/token` (client_credentials grant).

Missing for a real third-party-app OAuth provider: `GET /oauth/authorize` (auth-code flow entrypoint), consent UI, apps registry (`client_id`/`client_secret`/`redirect_uri`), auth-code → token exchange on `/oauth/token`, PKCE (RFC 7636), token introspection (RFC 7662), revoke (RFC 7009), refresh-token grant.

## Decision matrix

A. **Wrap Ory Hydra as a sidecar** — battle-tested (CF runs Hydra), full OAuth/OIDC; cost: new substrate dep, new SQL backend, duplicates trust-root concerns.

B. **Implement the spec slice in-stack** (~2-3k LOC TypeScript inside the existing notme Worker) — reuses notme's Ed25519 master for JWT issuance; trust root stays inside Interlace pipeline; ART takes responsibility for spec compliance. **Recommended.**

## Scope shape

`worker/src/oauth/` — authorize.ts, consent.ts, token.ts (extend existing), introspect.ts, revoke.ts, apps-registry.ts, auth-code-state.ts, pkce.ts. Cloister-side: extend `cloister.capnp` `identity-bridge` route paths under the same `wellKnownIdentityBridge` route kind (no new tenant; same trust boundary).

## Open decisions before implementation

1. Consent UI hosting: same Worker, or R2-hosted page + state callback? (Recommend: same Worker.)
2. Apps registry storage: new DO class, or extend notme's DO? (Recommend: extend existing.)
3. Token-lifetime defaults: align with CF's "multiple hours" or with Interlace's short-lease posture? (Recommend: short-lease Interlace-aligned.)
4. OAuth scopes: 1:1 mirror of Interlace scope vocabulary, or curated subset? (Recommend: 1:1 initially; add curation when external devs ask.)

## Why P2

Product-direction question, not substrate gap. ART works today with Interlace-only authn. The OAuth surface unlocks external developer adoption — ecosystem play, not a reliability fix. Land after substrate-trust layer is stable but before first external developer onboarding push.

## Full design

Staged at `docs/design/011-external-oauth-provider.md` (commit pending) — covers context, decision matrix, scope shape, file tree, all four open questions, and out-of-scope (SSO/SAML federation; centralized hosting; refresh-token leaked-token detection).

## Out of scope

- Replacing Interlace cert-based authn for internal substrate trust. Interlace stays the substrate-tier mechanism.
- SSO / SAML / corporate-IdP federation.
- Centralized hosting (à la Auth0 / Clerk). notme stays self-hosted by the cluster operator.

## Related

- https://blog.cloudflare.com/oauth-for-all/
- cloister.capnp identity-bridge tenant + ADR-0007 (Interlace), ADR-0018 (notme co-location)
- `~/remotes/art/notme/docs/design/011-external-oauth-provider.md` (staged)

title: P1: /authorize redirect mints DPoP-bound token — rejected by cnf check
description: /authorize page calls POST /token which mints a DPoP-bound token (cnf.jkt). After the cnf downgrade fix, verifyAccessToken correctly rejects tokens with cnf. The redirect flow is broken.\n\nFix: mint an unbound redirect token inside the DO (no cnf claim). Short-lived, single-use, EdDSA-signed. The /authorize page calls this instead of /token.

title: Expose JSON CABundle endpoint at /internal/ca-bundle for cloister consumption
description:
Surfaced 2026-05-09 from the cloister-side fetcher work (cloister-b89fdb).

## Background

cloister's lease middleware (cloister-bd7770) consumes a signed JSON `CABundle` to verify Signet ephemeral certs. The bundle shape is what notme already uses internally (`notme/worker/src/revocation.ts:CABundle`):

```
interface CABundle {
  epoch: number;
  seqno: number;
  keys: Record<string, string>;        // kid → b64-std raw Ed25519 pubkey
  keyId: string;
  prevKeyId?: string;
  issuedAt: number;                    // Unix-seconds
  signature: string;                   // Ed25519 over bundleCanonical, b64-std
}
```

Today notme exposes `/.well-known/ca-bundle.pem` (PEM-formatted X.509). cloister needs the raw JSON bundle (not PEM) because:
- The Interlace cert chain is Ed25519 raw-key, not X.509 hierarchies
- cloister's `bundleCanonical` (lifted from notme/revocation.ts) produces the canonical bytes that signet's Go side signs

## What to do

Add a service-binding-only endpoint at `/internal/ca-bundle` that:
1. Returns `Content-Type: application/json` with the current `CABundle` JSON
2. Calls `SIGNING_AUTHORITY.getCurrentCABundle()` (or whatever the existing internal accessor is named) to fetch the latest signed bundle
3. Sets `Cache-Control: public, max-age=240` (4 min — must stay strictly inside notme's `BUNDLE_MAX_AGE_MS = 5min` so cloister's 4-min refresh interval always sees a non-stale bundle; per cloister-e195ea audit amendment)
4. Returns 503 if no bundle is currently signed (cloister fails closed, then retries)

The endpoint MUST NOT be reachable from external HTTP (no Authorization-by-default-routes; restrict to service-binding callers via the existing internal-only path policy).

## Contract with cloister

cloister's fetcher: `cloister/src/storage/notme-bundle-fetcher.ts:notmeBundleFetcher`
- Calls `env.NOTME.fetch(new Request("https://notme-bot/internal/ca-bundle", { method: "GET" }))`
- Expects `200` + JSON body matching the CABundle shape
- Treats anything else as `null` (fail-closed via cloister's getCABundle)

cloister verifies the bundle's Ed25519 signature against `INTERLACE_ROOT_PUBKEY` after fetching, so this endpoint doesn't need to gate on the caller's identity — the signature is the trust anchor. But adding the service-binding restriction is defense-in-depth.

## Acceptance

- `/internal/ca-bundle` returns the current signed bundle as JSON
- The endpoint is unreachable from public HTTP (service-binding-only)
- A test in notme demonstrates signing the bundle once + serving it via the endpoint
- Cross-repo smoke: cloister's `task smoke` (when it runs against a notme replica) successfully fetches + verifies the bundle

## Files (notme-side)

- `notme/worker/worker.ts` — add the `/internal/ca-bundle` route
- `notme/worker/src/revocation.ts` — likely already has the bundle accessor; expose if needed
- `notme/worker/src/__tests__/internal-ca-bundle.test.ts` (NEW) — round-trip via the service binding

## Refs

- cloister-bd7770 — lease middleware (consumer)
- cloister-c614ae — bundle signature verification
- cloister-e195ea — CA bundle cache + 4-min refresh interval
- ADR-0007 audit amendment 2026-05-08 (cloister)

title: THREAT_MODEL claims the /authorize redirect token is DPoP-bound; it is an unbound bearer in a URL
description:
Found during adversarial review of PR #55 (notme-e1700d), 2026-08-03. NOT introduced by that PR — pre-existing on main.

THREAT_MODEL.md §5 (DPoP authorize redirect), row `token in URL logs`, states the mitigation as:

  "token is DPoP-bound (useless without ephemeral key), 5-min expiry, JTI unique"

The DPoP-bound half is FALSE, and it is the half doing the security work in that sentence.

Evidence chain, all verified at HEAD:

1. worker.ts:1814-1815 — the route's own comment: "POST /authorize/token — Unbound redirect token for /authorize flow. Session cookie required. No DPoP — token has no cnf.jkt."
2. worker.ts:1860 — the route calls `authority.mintRedirectToken(...)`, not the DPoP mint.
3. signing-authority.ts:433 — inside `mintRedirectToken`: "// No jkt — unbound token, accepted by verifyAccessToken". `mintAccessToken` only attaches `cnf` when `jkt` is truthy (auth/token.ts), so the minted JWT has no confirmation claim at all.
4. worker.ts:1866-1870 — responds `token_type: "Bearer"`.
5. worker.ts:926/933/937 — the `/authorize` page script then puts it in a URL and navigates:
     var token = data.access_token;
     var dest = redirectUri + sep + 'token=' + encodeURIComponent(token);
     window.location.href = dest;

So a plain bearer credential is written into a URL query parameter. Anyone who can read it from browser history, a Referer header, an intermediary proxy log, or the receiving server's own access log holds a working credential until it expires. "Useless without the ephemeral key" is exactly wrong: there is no key.

This is the defect class the project exists to eliminate — a bearer asset documented as proof-of-possession. The docs being wrong is worse than the code being weak, because the threat model is what a reviewer checks INSTEAD of re-deriving the property.

Mitigations that DO survive and should be what the row claims: 5-minute expiry, unique jti, audience allowlist (`getAllowedAudiences`, worker.ts:1843), and redirect_uri validation (`validateRedirectUri`, worker.ts:1776).

The comment at signing-authority.ts:422 gives the design reason the token is unbound — the /authorize flow's DPoP keypair is ephemeral and lost across the navigation — so this is a real constraint, not an oversight in the code. The bug is the threat model asserting a mitigation that was designed away.

Two things to do, in order:
1. CORRECT the THREAT_MODEL row to state the actual mitigations and name the residual exposure explicitly (bearer-in-URL, bounded by 5 min). Cheap, and it stops the false claim propagating.
2. THEN decide whether the residual is acceptable. Options if not: deliver via fragment (`#token=`) instead of query so it is not sent to the server or logged; POST the token to the redirect target instead of navigating; or a one-time exchange code redeemed by the receiving app (RFC 6749 §4.1 shape) so the URL carries a single-use code rather than the credential.

Related: docs/design/012-sender-constrained-oidc.md makes exactly this argument about id_tokens being bearer assertions. The same reasoning applies here and was not carried across.

comments.text:
CORRECTION to the fix in PR #56, caught before merge.

The first pass added `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` to the /authorize page and described it as stopping the browser from handing the token-bearing URL to third parties. **That was wrong and overstated the fix.**

A Referrer-Policy on a document governs the Referer THAT document sends — its own subresource loads, and the navigation away to redirect_uri. It does not govern what the DESTINATION page sends once the browser is sitting on `${redirect_uri}?token=...`. That is the destination's own Referrer-Policy (rig's), and it is the vector that actually forwards the access token onward. notme cannot close it from the /authorize page.

What the header does protect: the authorize URL itself, which carries `state` (a CSRF value), from being sent onward. Modest — modern browsers default to `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` and would send only the origin anyway, so this mostly makes an existing default explicit and covers the same-origin case. Keeping it (correct hygiene), but it is NOT a mitigation for this row and the comment, threat-model row and test now say so.

BLAST RADIUS, now established concretely. One consumer: `rig/web/src/index.ts:396` redirects to `auth.notme.bot/authorize` for the `/admin/setup-github` flow, and line 355 reads the token back with `c.req.query('token')` — a SERVER-SIDE query read. Consequences:

- The token reaches rig's Cloudflare Worker in the request line, so it lands in Cloudflare's access logs. This is the largest unmitigated vector, larger than the Referer one.
- A fragment-based fix (`#token=`) would BREAK rig outright — fragments never reach the server. rig would need client-side JS to read `location.hash` and hand it over out-of-band.

Corrected residual, all unmitigated:
1. Token in browser history on the user's machine.
2. Token in the destination's server/access logs (verified above).
3. Onward Referer leakage from the destination page — governed by rig, not notme.

Bounding facts that keep this moderate rather than critical: 5-minute lifetime; `aud` pins it to ONE resource server so it is not a general-purpose credential; unique jti; it is an access token, not a session, so it cannot be used to mint more; and the flow is a rarely-exercised admin path.

Options to actually remove it, ranked:
1. **Single-use exchange code** (RFC 6749 §4.1). The URL carries a code, not a credential; a logged code is worthless once redeemed. Correct long-term shape and where ADR-011 already points (it lists `/oauth/authorize` + code exchange as missing). Needs a rig change.
2. **Fragment** (`#token=`). Removes vectors 2 and 3 outright — fragments are never sent to servers and never appear in a Referer. Cheapest real improvement. Needs a rig change (server-side read becomes client-side).
3. **POST-to-target** (auto-submitting form). Token in a body, not a URL. Needs a rig change.

All three are coordinated cross-repo changes. Not doing any of them unilaterally — filing the decision here. Recommend (1) since ADR-011 is already headed there, with (2) as a stopgap if the admin flow needs hardening sooner.

title: notme: per-issuer audience map for OIDC providers (Google etc.)
CORS preflight advertises cross-origin /token, but no /token response carries Access-Control-Allow-Origin
description:
Found during adversarial review of PR #55 (notme-e1700d), 2026-08-03. Pre-existing on main; PR #55 fixed the adjacent Expose-Headers gap for its own nonce header but deliberately did not widen scope to this.

The OPTIONS preflight (worker.ts:1272-1281) advertises cross-origin support in detail:
- `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: <requestOrigin>` for an allowlist of rosary.bot, auth.rosary.bot, notme.bot, auth.notme.bot, mcp.rosary.bot, mache.rosary.bot, plus http://localhost:*
- `Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, OPTIONS`
- `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization, DPoP`

The `DPoP` entry means cross-origin DPoP-authenticated POSTs are the explicit intent.

But `grep -n corsAllowed worker.ts` and `grep -n requestOrigin worker.ts` both return hits ONLY inside that OPTIONS branch. No actual (non-preflight) response computes or emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. The `/token` route returns bare `Response.json(...)`. The only ACAO values elsewhere in the file are hardcoded `"*"` on public well-known documents (worker.ts:1191, 2076, 2107, 2163, 2215) — jwks.json and friends — not on /token.

Consequence: a browser at https://rosary.bot doing `fetch('https://auth.notme.bot/token', {method:'POST', headers:{DPoP: proof}})` passes preflight and then has the response blocked, because the actual response has no ACAO. The preflight is writing a cheque the response does not honour.

Compounding: /token requires the `notme_session` cookie (worker.ts:1926-1934), and cross-origin cookie sending requires BOTH `credentials: 'include'` client-side and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` server-side. The latter is absent — and THREAT_MODEL.md §7 records that as deliberate: "Access-Control-Allow-Credentials not set (DPoP tokens used instead of cookies cross-origin)". So the cookie could not be sent cross-origin even if ACAO were fixed.

That makes this a DESIGN question, not a one-line fix, which is why it is filed rather than patched:

Either (a) cross-origin /token is genuinely intended — then it needs ACAO on the response, a credentials story that does not contradict the §7 threat-model row (e.g. accept the session via an Authorization header rather than a cookie), and a test; or (b) /token is same-origin only — then the preflight should stop advertising `DPoP` in Allow-Headers for it, because the current state tells an integrator the flow works when it cannot.

Determine which before writing code. ADR-006 says browser flows are the whole reason /token still exists ("admin pages like rosary.bot/admin/setup-github"), and rosary.bot is a DIFFERENT origin from auth.notme.bot — which suggests (a) was the intent and was never completed.

Verify with: `grep -n "corsAllowed\|requestOrigin\|Access-Control" worker/worker.ts`
acceptance_criteria: Decision recorded (cross-origin /token supported, or preflight narrowed to stop advertising it). If supported: a test asserts a /token response carries Access-Control-Allow-Origin for an allowlisted origin and that the credentials story does not contradict THREAT_MODEL §7. `task worker:check` green.

title: Audit notme.bot ecosystem representation and stale APAS route
description: Map the rig front-end and the notme.bot/apas content against APAS in agentic-research/signet plus rosary, ley-line-open, and cloister; identify stale claims and missing ecosystem relationships; recommend or implement scoped corrections once current state is understood.

comments.text: Audit findings: live site source is notme/worker/public, not ../rig/notme (which only has an orphaned getting-started page + task stub). worker/public/apas.html is stale at APAS 0.1.0-draft (2026-03-25) while signet main is 0.2.0-draft (2026-05-09). Page incorrectly says DSSE is not yet shipped, uses normative beadRef/agent terminology superseded by workItemRef/dispatch, and omits rosary, ley-line-open, rig, and cloister from the implementation map. Homepage likewise says DSSE signing is coming. Current architecture: signet = identity primitives + spec home; notme/auth.notme.bot = identity authority + APAS predicate namespace; rosary = orchestrator/reference implementation and shipped L1/partial L2; ley-line-open = shared signing/CAS substrate; rig = deployment/compute plane; cloister = isolated delivery/audit/credential plane and emerging L3 substrate.
comments.author: rsry-cli

comments.text: Expanded reality check across sibling repos. ley-line-open has no direct APAS/DSSE/in-toto implementation; it ships leyline-sign (CMS/PKCS#7 Ed25519, cert-chain verification, sign-only host helper) and signed Merkle-CAS Heads. Rosary's APAS DSSE path still uses ed25519-dalek directly, so LLO is supporting signing/storage substrate and consolidation target, not the current APAS envelope signer. title: Declare notme-396aff's LLO wasm-artifact wait in a local .vigil.toml
description:
Move this repo's cross-repo wait out of vigil's central config and into a
`.vigil.toml` fragment here, so the repo that OWNS the wait declares it.

## Mechanism (already exists, verified in vigil src/config.rs)

vigil's global config carries `repos = [...]`; each adopted directory
contributes its own `[[watches]]` from a `.vigil.toml` at its root.
`load_effective_config` applies per-repo defaults:

    if watch.repo.local_path.is_none() && watch.repo.remote.is_none() {
        watch.repo.local_path = Some(repo_dir.clone());   // only if BOTH unset
    }
    if watch.bead_repo.is_none() && !watch.bead_ids.is_empty() {
        watch.bead_repo = Some(repo_dir.clone());         // this repo's own store
    }

That fits a cross-repo wait exactly: set `repo.remote` explicitly (which
suppresses the local_path default) and `bead_repo` correctly falls back to
THIS repo. Duplicate watch names across sources are refused loudly, naming
both files. Fragments cannot adopt further repos — no recursion.

## Why it is better than the central file

Today vigil's watches.toml would have to know this repo's bead ids. That is
central inference about someone else's state. A fragment is authored by the
repo that actually holds the bead, versioned in ITS history, and moves with
it. Same discipline as the rest of the release-contract work: declare
locally, do not infer centrally.

## Verify before arming

`vigil run --config <path> --dry-run` reads for real (gh, crates.io, the
bead store) and writes nothing. A watch that would act prints
`WOULD notify <bead-id> (<evidence>)`. Check that line names the right bead
and carries evidence you believe before this fragment goes live.

Caveat: `--dry-run` prints `UNCHECKED` for merge_shaped watches. git_pull's
check IS its pull, so a dry run genuinely cannot exercise that path. Only
tool_poll conditions are verified by it.

## Note on on_resolve

Default is `Close`. For a bead that is BLOCKED-class — real work that could
not start until an external fact was true — use `on_resolve = "comment"`.
Closing such a bead destroys the work item rather than completing it. See
vigil-cbbed3: the default is destructive-on-omission and is being changed.

## This repo's watch

notme-396aff waits on the same ley-line-open v0.14.0 wasm artifacts as
signet-3a6a7c. Two beads, two stores, one external fact — which is exactly
why they are two watches rather than one with two bead_ids: `bead_repo` is
per-watch, so beads in different stores cannot share one.

ALREADY TRUE as of 2026-08-04. v0.14.0 published 2026-07-31T05:23:48Z with
all four assets attached. `vigil run --dry-run` printed:

    llo v0.14.0 wasm assets (notme): WOULD notify notme-396aff (release
    v0.14.0 published 2026-07-31T05:23:48Z carries all 4 declared assets (...))

    [[watches]]
    name = "notme: llo wasm artifacts"
    bead_ids = ["notme-396aff"]
    on_resolve = "comment"
    [watches.repo]
    remote = "agentic-research/ley-line-open"
    [watches.condition]
    type = "release_assets"
    tag = "v0.14.0"
    assets = ["leyline_sign.wasm", "leyline_cas_ffi.wasm", "leyline_envelope.wasm", "SHA256SUMS"]
acceptance_criteria: A .vigil.toml exists at notme root declaring the LLO wasm-artifact watch with on_resolve = "comment"; `vigil run --dry-run` prints a WOULD notify line naming notme-396aff; the directory is listed in vigil watches.toml `repos`.

title: bug(dpop): enforce proof alg/key pairing and reject private JWK material

title: Templatize _api-docs.html instead of runtime string-replacing the production host
description:
Found by adversarial review of PR #71 (goal notme-cf288e). worker/worker.ts's /api/docs handler decodes the static `_api-docs` asset and does `html.replaceAll("auth.notme.bot", authorityHost)` when serving a non-production environment, so a staging deploy doesn't render production URLs (the config-leak check in worker:verify).

Correct and zero-risk as shipped — production is fully guarded off (the condition is false when SIGNET_AUTHORITY_URL is unset or names auth.notme.bot), header handling after the .text() decode is right, and the response stays cache-partitioned per host. But it is a bandage: worker/public/_api-docs.html hardcodes auth.notme.bot in ~10 places (title, canonical link, curl examples, discovery JSON), and the rewrite couples worker.ts to that literal domain string. A future domain change requires editing both the HTML and the literal in worker.ts, and the coupling is invisible from either side.

Fix: substitute a placeholder token (e.g. {{AUTHORITY_HOST}}) in the asset at request or build time instead of matching the literal production domain. Pre-existing debt in the asset, surfaced rather than caused by this change.
acceptance_criteria: worker/public/_api-docs.html contains no hardcoded production authority host; /api/docs renders the serving environment's host in both production and staging; `task worker:verify` and `task worker:verify-staging` both pass their api-docs check.

title: red-team:trust-root — staging authority mints access tokens claiming iss=https://auth.notme.bot (hardcoded ISSUER), contradicting ADR-018's own exit criterion
description:
red-team:trust-root — filed from adversarial review of PR #70 (origin/goalzero, ADR-018 staging + canary promotion).

## Location
- `worker/src/auth/token.ts:16` — `const ISSUER = "https://auth.notme.bot";`
- `worker/src/auth/token.ts:64` — `iss: ISSUER` in every minted access token
- Callers: `worker/src/signing-authority.ts:574` and `:1040` (`mintAccessToken`)
- Contradicted claim: `docs/design/018-goal-zero-promotion.md`, Phase 1 exit criteria — "Staging discovery serves `"issuer": "https://auth-staging.notme.bot"`"

## Required attacker capability
NONE. This is the default behavior of the environment PR #70 introduces. No attacker is needed to produce the confusable object; an attacker is only needed to find a verifier that accepts it.

## Compromise path
PR #70 adds `[env.staging]` — a separate Worker (`notme-bot-staging`) with its OWN `SigningAuthority` DO, therefore its own independently-born Ed25519 master key, serving `/token` on the public host `auth-staging.notme.bot`.

`ISSUER` is a module constant, not derived from `env.SIGNET_AUTHORITY_URL`. So:

1. The staging worker's `/.well-known/signet-authority.json` and `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` correctly advertise `issuer: https://auth-staging.notme.bot` (worker.ts:2874, :2941 — both use `authorityUrl`, which IS env-derived).
2. The tokens that same worker mints assert `iss: "https://auth.notme.bot"` — the PRODUCTION issuer — signed with the STAGING key.

Two consequences, in opposite directions:

**(a) Forged issuer identity.** A staging-minted token is a bearer object asserting production provenance. Any verifier whose key-resolution path can reach the staging key (a JWKS union, a "point the client at staging to test" config, an operator who pastes the staging kid into an allowlist) will accept a staging token as a production token. The staging JWKS is public and unauthenticated at `https://auth-staging.notme.bot/.well-known/jwks.json`, so the key half is free to obtain.

**(b) Staging cannot faithfully exercise the production token path.** An RFC 8414 §2-conformant client does discovery against staging, learns `issuer: https://auth-staging.notme.bot`, receives a token with `iss: https://auth.notme.bot`, and MUST reject it on issuer mismatch. So ADR-018's own Phase 1 gate — "For identity-critical changes ... a manual token-path exercise against staging (`/token` DPoP flow)" — either fails spuriously, or is performed with a client that skips `iss` validation, which means the gate does not test what it claims to test.

This also violates RFC 8414 §2 (metadata `issuer` MUST equal the `iss` of tokens the server issues) and defeats RFC 9207 issuer identification.

## What currently holds (and why it is not a defense)
No live verifier is confusable TODAY, but by accident of incompleteness rather than by design:
- cloister `src/routes/bundle-auth.ts:100-101,144` requires a caller-supplied `notmePub`; the `kid`→key resolver (`src/routes/notme-jwks.ts`) does not exist, and `authenticateBundleRequest` has no production caller (`src/vault-store.ts:113-117` documents it as unwired).
- signet's `staticKeyProvider` (`pkg/http/middleware/options.go:169-178`) ignores `issuerID` entirely and returns the single `WithMasterKey` key.
- A verifier that fetches JWKS from exactly the token's `iss` gets production's JWKS and fails the signature check.

Every one of those is "the confusable code path was never built." ADR-018 tells a future integrator that staging's issuer is distinct, so the integrator who builds the kid-resolver against that documented (false) invariant builds the confusable verifier.

## Detection
None. `task worker:verify-staging` only asserts `/token` returns 400 `dpop_proof_required` (Taskfile.yml, `check_request "token"`) — it never mints a token or inspects `iss`. `docs:check` validates bead citations and endpoint lists, not claim-vs-constant.

## Recovery
If a staging token is accepted as production somewhere: revoke by rotating the staging DO key (destroys nothing production-side), and audit the accepting verifier's key set. Recovery is cheap precisely because the staging CA is worthless — which is the argument for making the token SAY so.

## Closing playbook (minimal correction)
1. Derive the issuer from config instead of hardcoding: thread `authorityUrl` (already computed at worker.ts:1663-1664 from `env.SIGNET_AUTHORITY_URL`) into `mintAccessToken` as an `issuer` param, defaulting to `https://auth.notme.bot` when unset. `signing-authority.ts:574` and `:1040` are the only two call sites.
2. Add a unit test asserting `iss` in a minted token equals the `issuer` field of the AS metadata document built for the same env — i.e. pin RFC 8414 §2 self-consistency, not a literal.
3. Extend `worker:verify` with a check that discovery's `issuer` equals `${AUTH_BASE}`, so a future divergence fails the staging gate rather than passing it.

## Confidence
High. The constant, the two call sites, the env-derived metadata issuer, and the ADR claim were each read directly.

Re-verified at `41d4f46` (after the two security-review rounds: `b25ff5e`, `eb8964f`, `66a7461`, `dc24f69`, `41d4f46`). **Unchanged and still live.**

- `worker/src/auth/token.ts:16` — `const ISSUER = "https://auth.notme.bot";`

- `docs/design/018-goal-zero-promotion.md:83` still asserts staging discovery serves `"issuer": "https://auth-staging.notme.bot"`, and `:92` still says the staging CA "is not trusted by anything".

## New evidence found this round — the constant is load-bearing on the VERIFY side too

`token.ts:133`, inside `verifyAccessToken`:

```ts
validateClaims(payload, {
  issuer: ISSUER,
});
```

So the staging Worker's own verifier pins the issuer to the hardcoded production string. Two consequences that sharpen the original finding:

1. **Staging is internally self-consistent while being externally a liar.** It mints `iss: https://auth.notme.bot` and it validates `iss === https://auth.notme.bot`, so every staging-local test passes. Nothing inside the staging environment can surface the mismatch — which is exactly why ADR-018's Phase 1 "manual token-path exercise against staging" would come back green while proving nothing about issuer identity.
2. **A production-issued token clears staging's issuer check** and fails only at the signature step (different keys). The issuer claim is doing no isolation work in either direction.

## Correction to the fix scope

The original playbook said "thread `authorityUrl` into `mintAccessToken`." That is now incomplete — `verifyAccessToken` needs the same treatment, or the two halves drift and staging starts rejecting its own tokens. Both call sites of the constant must move to config together:

- mint: `signing-authority.ts:574`, `:1040`
- verify: `token.ts:133`

The acceptance criterion on this bead already covers the mint side; extend it to assert the verify side uses the same resolved value.

DUPLICATE of notme-28baf2, which is FIXED and closed — closing this one for the same reason rather than leaving two open beads for one defect.

Both describe the same defect: worker/src/auth/token.ts held `const ISSUER = "https://auth.notme.bot"` used for BOTH minting and verifying, so staging advertised issuer https://auth-staging.notme.bot in its env-derived discovery document while minting tokens asserting the production issuer, signed with the staging key (RFC 8414 §2). Because verify read the same constant, staging was internally self-consistent while externally lying, and a staging token-path exercise came back green while proving nothing about issuer identity.

The duplication is mine: this bead was filed by the trust-root review, and I filed notme-28baf2 for the same finding before reconciling against the existing red-team beads. Worth noting as a process gap — the red-team beads (red-team:trust-root prefix) were not in my search path when I filed follow-ups.

Making it required rather than defaulted is what found both DO mint sites — the type checker, not a search. Verified live: staging's discovery document now reports issuer https://auth-staging.notme.bot with tokens to match. The load-bearing test is the cross-environment one — a production-issuer token is rejected under the staging issuer, while the same token with the same key and correct issuer is accepted, proving the rejection is the issuer check and not a signature failure doing the work.

See notme-28baf2 for the full record.

title: red-team:trust-root — the staging CA is name-identical to production: same WIMSE trust domain, same CA subject DN, same GHA owner scope, production audience allowlist
description:
red-team:trust-root — filed from adversarial review of PR #70 (origin/goalzero, ADR-018).

ADR-018 asserts "Staging state is disposable by design (its CA is not trusted by anything)." That is true of the KEY and false of every NAME the CA emits. A staging-minted credential is string-identical to a production one in every field a verifier reads except the raw key bytes.

## Location — four independent name collisions
1. **WIMSE trust domain is a literal, not env-derived.** All three mint paths hardcode `notme.bot`:
   - `worker/worker.ts:753` — `wimse://notme.bot/gha/${owner}/${repo}` (GHA OIDC path)
   - `worker/worker.ts:2272` — `wimse://notme.bot/${authMethod}/${principalId}` (touched by PR #71, hardcode retained)
   - `worker/src/cert-exchange.ts:208` — `wimse://notme.bot/${authMethod}/${principalId}`
2. **CA subject DN is a literal.** `worker/src/signing-authority.ts:514` — `name: "CN=signet-authority,O=notme"`. The staging self-signed CA cert carries a byte-identical subject/issuer to production's.
3. **GHA owner scope is identical and cannot fail closed by omission.** Live `worker/wrangler.toml:37` and `:116` both set `GHA_ALLOWED_OWNERS = "agentic-research"`; worse, `worker/worker.ts:575` defaults to `env.GHA_ALLOWED_OWNERS ?? "agentic-research"`, so deleting the staging var does not narrow the scope — it re-supplies the production org.
4. **Staging inherits the PRODUCTION audience allowlist.** `[env.staging.vars]` sets no `ALLOWED_AUDIENCES`, so `getAllowedAudiences` (`worker/src/allowed-audiences.ts:24-33`) falls back to `DEFAULT_ALLOWED_AUDIENCES` — `https://rosary.bot`, `https://mcp.rosary.bot`, `https://mache.rosary.bot`, `https://notme.bot`, `https://auth.notme.bot`. Staging will happily mint tokens scoped to production resource servers.

`/cert/gha` (worker.ts:2299) sits inside the authority-surface block, which PR #70's `authorityHostFromEnv` now selects on `auth-staging.notme.bot` — so staging serves the GHA cert-exchange endpoint on a public hostname under the production registrable domain.

## Required attacker capability
A GitHub Actions workflow in the `agentic-research` org — i.e. any contributor who can land a workflow file, plus anyone who already has that. No CF account access, no filesystem write, no config write.

## Compromise path
1. Attacker's workflow presents its GHA OIDC token to `https://auth-staging.notme.bot/cert/gha`.
2. `getAllowedOwners` accepts `agentic-research` (staging and prod agree).
3. Staging mints a bridge cert pair: identity `wimse://notme.bot/gha/agentic-research/<repo>`, chaining to a CA whose subject is `CN=signet-authority,O=notme`, valid 10 years.
4. The attacker now holds a self-consistent (leaf, CA-bundle) pair, both fetchable from the same public origin, that is indistinguishable from production output by NAME.
5. Any verifier that authorizes on the identity string, the issuer DN, or "fetch the bundle from the authority that issued the leaf" accepts it.

Step 5 is not hypothetical. `signet/cmd/sigstore-kms-signet/enroll.go:185-207` fetches the CA bundle PEM from the *same authority URL* that just issued the leaf and verifies the leaf against that pool — same-origin TOFU with no out-of-band anchor. `--authority-url` (default `https://auth.notme.bot`, `sign_artifact.go:16`) is the only thing choosing which CA; pointing it at staging yields a fully self-verifying chain. `sign_artifact.go:194-208` then hands cosign `--certificate-identity <identity>` — an exact string match on a value that staging can reproduce byte-for-byte.

## What holds, and why it is thinner than it looks
Cloister verifies bundles by **raw key bytes**, not names — `src/storage/ca-bundle-cache.ts:154-163` verifies the Ed25519 signature against `INTERLACE_ROOT_PUBKEY`, and `src/routes/lease-middleware.ts:357-364` extracts `bundle.keys[bundle.keyId]` rather than reading any DN. `src/storage/ca-bundle-source.ts:58-67` fails closed (`CaUnavailableError`) when the pubkey is unset. That is the right design and it genuinely defeats this attack for cloister's live path — credit where due.

But the residual is real: `ca-bundle-cache.ts:164-178` still SKIPS verification when `rootPubkey` is empty, logging `outcome: "skipped_unverified"`, and `getCABundle` is exported without the `resolveCABundle` guard. Cloister ships `INTERLACE_ROOT_PUBKEY = ""` in `wrangler.toml:165`. A cloister staging deployment pointed at `notme-bot-staging` with the pubkey left blank silently adopts the staging CA as its trust root.

## Detection
None. Nothing in the substrate distinguishes a staging-issued cert from a production one after the fact: no environment marker in the identity URI, no distinguishing name or extension in the CA cert, no separate serial namespace. An auditor holding a leaf cert cannot tell which CA minted it without already possessing both public keys.

## Recovery
Rotating the staging DO key invalidates staging-issued leaves — but only for verifiers that pin keys. A verifier that was fooled by NAME never learns anything changed. There is no revocation story for "a cert with a legitimate-looking identity signed by the wrong root," because the substrate has no concept of which root is which.

## Closing playbook (minimal correction, in order of cost)
1. **Make the trust domain env-derived.** Replace the three `wimse://notme.bot/` literals with the host from `SITE_URL` (or a new `WIMSE_TRUST_DOMAIN` var), so staging emits `wimse://staging.notme.bot/...`. This is the single highest-value change: it makes the identity self-describing and every name-based verifier fails closed automatically.
2. **Distinguish the CA subject.** Derive the DN from the authority host — `CN=signet-authority-staging,O=notme` — so an X.509 verifier can tell them apart, and add an environment marker to the bundle.
3. **Scope staging's authority explicitly.** Set `ALLOWED_AUDIENCES` in `[env.staging.vars]` to staging-only values, and set `GHA_ALLOWED_OWNERS` to an org that does not exist in production (and remove the `?? "agentic-research"` default at worker.ts:575 so omission fails closed rather than inheriting production).
4. **Consider a separate registrable domain for staging.** Sharing `notme.bot` means the two roots are separated by hostname alone, and hostname is exactly what the identity strings decline to record. A distinct zone would make the confusion structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged. This is the "do it properly" option; items 1-3 are the cheap ones that close the concrete path.
5. **Close cloister's fail-open branch** (cross-repo): make an empty `rootPubkey` an error in `getCABundle`, not a skip.

## Confidence
High for items 1-3 (read directly from the live `worker/wrangler.toml` and source). High for the signet enroll path (read at file:line). Medium on the cloister fail-open branch being reachable in practice — the live caller is guarded; the export is not.

title: red-team:trust-root — authorityHostFromEnv returns "" (not null) for hostless URL schemes, matching an empty Host header onto the authority surface
description:
red-team:trust-root — filed from adversarial review of PR #70 (origin/goalzero).

## Location
- `worker/worker.ts:1445-1453` — `authorityHostFromEnv()`
- `worker/worker.ts:1644` — canonical-host redirect, guarded by `host !== ""`
- `worker/worker.ts:1661-1662` — `authorityHost !== null && host === authorityHost`

## The defect
The helper treats "URL parses" as "URL names a host". It does not. Verified against Node's WHATWG URL parser:

```
file:///x            => host ""     (not a throw)
about:blank          => host ""
data:text/plain,hi   => host ""
javascript:alert(1)  => host ""
mailto:a@b.c         => host ""
foo:bar              => host ""
https://a@evil.com   => host "evil.com"   (userinfo stripped, host is real)
https://[::1]:8788   => host "[::1]:8788"
```

Only a genuine parse failure yields `null`. Every scheme above returns the empty string, which is `!== null`, so the guard at :1662 reduces to `host === ""`.

This composes badly with the canonical-host redirect at :1644, which deliberately exempts the empty host (`&& host !== ""`) so that health probes from bare-IP origins are not redirected. The two exemptions meet: a request with an absent or empty `Host` header skips canonicalization AND satisfies the authority-host comparison, so it is served the full identity-authority surface — `/cert`, `/cert/gha`, `/token`, `/auth/passkey/*`.

## Required attacker capability
Config-write on `SIGNET_AUTHORITY_URL` (operator error or a compromised deploy config), PLUS the ability to reach the Worker with an empty Host header. On the Cloudflare edge the second half is not reachable from the public internet — CF populates `Host`/`:authority` on every request. It is reachable in local workerd and plausibly through non-CF fronting. So this is a fail-open in a guard that should be fail-closed, not a live exploit.

## Why it still matters
PR #70 promotes `SIGNET_AUTHORITY_URL` from a display/origin value to a **routing decision**. Before this change a malformed value broke WebAuthn (it is the RP origin at worker.ts:815-818) and the discovery documents, but could not change which host serves the authority. Now one env var does quadruple duty — WebAuthn RP ID + origin, discovery `issuer`, AS-metadata `issuer`, and authority-surface host selection — and nothing validates it. There is no scheme check either: `SIGNET_AUTHORITY_URL=http://...` is accepted and becomes the advertised HTTPS-less issuer.

Adjacent, checked and clear: an uppercase Host header fails closed (`getSubdomain`'s regex at :1432 is case-sensitive and the `endsWith("notme.bot")` test at :1644 fails, so the request is 301'd). A trailing-dot value (`https://auth.notme.bot.`) also fails closed the same way. Ports and userinfo behave correctly.

## Detection
None — a request served the authority surface on an unintended host is indistinguishable in logs from a legitimate one.

## Closing playbook
In `authorityHostFromEnv`, reject anything that is not an https (or, for local dev, http) URL with a non-empty host:

```ts
const u = new URL(signetAuthorityUrl);
if (u.protocol !== "https:" && u.protocol !== "http:") return null;
return u.host || null;
```

Add the three cases to `worker/src/__tests__/authority-host.test.ts` — `file:///x`, `about:blank`, and `http://` on a non-localhost host — asserting `null`. The existing test file covers the malformed-string case (`"not a url"`) but not the parses-but-hostless class, which is why this survived.

## Confidence
High on the parser behavior (executed, output above). High on the code path. Low on public-internet reachability, which is why this is a fix-now-cheaply rather than a merge blocker.
acceptance_criteria: authorityHostFromEnv returns null for URLs that parse but carry no host (file:, about:, data:, mailto:, javascript:, opaque schemes) and for non-http(s) protocols. worker/src/__tests__/authority-host.test.ts asserts null for "file:///x" and "about:blank". `cd worker && pnpm exec vitest run src/__tests__/authority-host.test.ts` green.

title: red-team:trust-root — the canonical fixture gate has no integrity anchor: self-referential in notme, unconsumed elsewhere, and .bin is never checked against .expected.hex
description:
red-team:trust-root — filed from adversarial review of PR #71 (origin/fix/notme-92a1b9-bootstrap, notme-e9d2b8). Assesses `schema/fixtures/` AS A TRUST ROOT, not as a test.

The fixtures are correct. I verified `cabundle-basic.expected.hex` (`a60101020103a1636b696442abcd04636b69640560061904d2`, 25 bytes) and `cabundle-multikey.expected.hex` decode to exactly the RFC 8949 §4.2 canonical encodings the README describes, including the load-bearing length-then-bytewise ordering that puts `"b"` before `"ab"`. The concern is not the bytes; it is what defends them.

## Location
- `schema/fixtures/{cabundle-basic,cabundle-multikey}.{json,expected.hex,bin}`
- `schema/fixtures/README.md` — "Never edit `.expected.hex`/`.bin` to make a failing implementation pass"
- `worker/src/__tests__/bundle-canonical.test.ts:29-56` (`loadFixture`), `:126`, `:147`

## Three gaps

**1. The rule is prose, and prose is not a gate.** The README's "never edit expected to make a failing impl pass" is enforced by nothing. A PR that edits `revocation.ts`'s encoder AND `cabundle-basic.expected.hex` in the same commit is green. The fixture is a *within-repo* restatement of the implementation's own output, so it cannot detect a change to that implementation — only an accidental one.

**2. No consumer outside notme, so the cross-implementation claim is currently false.** The README says signet and ley-line-open "should consume these files." Neither does:
- signet has no `schema/`, no `fixtures/`, no `.gitmodules`, no copy script. `pkg/revocation/canonical_test.go:103-133` asserts a hand-inlined `[]byte{0xa6, 0x01, ...}` whose comment says it is "mirrored byte-for-byte" from notme — a manual copy with no sync mechanism. `signet/docs/design/cross-language-schema.md:131` states the lift is a future bead.
- ley-line-open has no CBOR dependency in `rs/ll-open/sign/` at all; its own bead `ley-line-open-0466c0` ("Consume notme's schema/fixtures canonical CBOR fixtures") is still open.
- cloister's `src/storage/bundle-canonical.ts:6-8` claims it "must stay byte-equal with notme's encoder," but `test/storage/bundle-canonical.test.ts` has no golden vector — all 15 cases are self-consistency.

So today three implementations each verify their own determinism, and byte-equality between them is asserted by comment. Landing the fixtures is real progress; the gate they were supposed to close is not closed yet.

**3. `.bin` is dead weight that a consumer may trust.** `loadFixture` reads only `.json` and `.expected.hex` (`bundle-canonical.test.ts:38-51`). Nothing anywhere asserts `cabundle-basic.bin == hex_decode(cabundle-basic.expected.hex)`. A Go or Rust consumer that reads the raw `.bin` (the natural choice — no hex decoding) would be trusting a file that no CI job has ever looked at. That is a genuine substitution surface: edit only `.bin`, every notme test stays green, and the downstream consumer silently gets different bytes.

## Required attacker capability
A merged PR — i.e. the capability of any contributor whose change reaches `main`. This is the ordinary supply-chain position, not a privileged one.

## What the attacker achieves
Editing `.expected.hex` alone: nothing (the test fails). Editing impl + `.expected.hex` together: the canonical encoding silently changes, and once signet/LLO adopt the files, all three converge on the attacker's encoding — which is worth having, because the canonical bytes ARE the Ed25519 signing input for every CA bundle. A divergence there is not a test failure; it is a signature-verification split-brain across the trust fabric. Editing `.bin` alone: today, nothing observable; after adoption, a targeted divergence in exactly one consumer.

## Detection
CI catches only the impl-only and hex-only edits. The paired edit and the `.bin`-only edit are invisible. There is no CODEOWNERS entry on `schema/fixtures/`, no signature, no checksum manifest.

## Closing playbook
1. **Assert `.bin` in the test.** One line in `loadFixture` — read `.bin`, assert it equals the hex-decoded `.expected.hex`. Closes gap 3 immediately and costs nothing.
2. **Make the paired edit visible rather than preventable.** A checksum manifest (`schema/fixtures/SHA256SUMS`) does not stop a PR that also updates the manifest, but it turns a silent two-file edit into a three-file edit that names itself in the diff. Add `CODEOWNERS` on `schema/fixtures/**` so the change requires a specific reviewer. That is the honest ceiling for in-repo fixtures — the real anchor has to be external.
3. **The real anchor: derive the vector independently.** The multikey fixture's value is that it encodes a *rule* (RFC 8949 §4.2 ordering), so a property test — generate random key maps, assert the encoder's output ordering matches an independently-implemented comparator — catches an encoder change that a golden file cannot, because it does not share the encoder's provenance.
4. **Cross-repo consumption should vendor-with-checksum, not submodule.** ley-line-open already has exactly this pattern working for a different upstream: `rs/ll-core/mcp-protocol-schema/build.rs:129-135` generates `PINNED_REVISION` + `PINNED_SHA256`, gated by `tests/protocol_schema_pin.rs:97-108`. Copy that shape. A submodule pins a commit but re-verifies nothing; a vendored copy plus a recorded digest makes an upstream edit a compile-time failure in the consumer, which is the property you want — the consumer should have to *acknowledge* an encoding change, not silently inherit it.

## Confidence
High. Fixture bytes decoded and verified by hand; the three consumer repos searched directly for `.gitmodules`, copy scripts, checksum manifests, and fixture filenames, with none found.
acceptance_criteria: bundle-canonical.test.ts asserts each fixture's .bin equals hex_decode(.expected.hex); a property test asserts RFC 8949 §4.2 key ordering over generated key maps rather than only the two golden vectors. `cd worker && pnpm exec vitest run src/__tests__/bundle-canonical.test.ts` green.

title: Audit + ship OCI image `notme:0.1.0` consumable by cloister cluster.capnp
description:
Filed 2026-05-10 from cloister's deployment-readiness audit.

## What needs to happen

cloister's `cluster.capnp` (the multi-bundle deployment manifest at `~/remotes/art/cloister/cluster.capnp`) expects an OCI image tagged **`notme:0.1.0`** for the `notme-identity` bundle. cloister's `task cluster:up` invokes a compose runtime (nerdctl/podman/docker) and assumes this image is locally available (or pullable from a registry).

Today notme has apko + melange configs at:
- `packages/apko-notme.yaml`
- `packages/melange-workerd.yaml`
- `packages/melange-notme-app.yaml`

But it's not clear from outside notme whether `task image` (or equivalent) actually:
1. Produces an image tagged `notme:0.1.0`.
2. Bundles the worker (`worker/dist/`) into the image at a path workerd can boot from.
3. Embeds `worker/wrangler.toml`-equivalent config that lets it serve on port 8788 (the port cluster.capnp expects).
4. Survives `docker load < notme.tar` + `docker run -p 8788:8788 notme:0.1.0` → 200 on `/health`.

## Acceptance

- `task image` (or whatever the build target is — name it if different) produces `notme.tar` or pushes to a local registry.
- `docker load < notme.tar` (or pull) makes `notme:0.1.0` available locally.
- `docker run -p 8788:8788 notme:0.1.0` boots and responds 200 on `/health` (or notme's equivalent liveness endpoint).
- Document the build invocation in notme's README so a cloister operator can reproduce it.
- If the apko configs need updates (version pin, port, entrypoint), update them.
- If notme has its OWN cluster.capnp / equivalent topology, mention how the two compose (cross-link).

## Cross-repo context

- **cloister** at `~/remotes/art/cloister/cluster.capnp` declares `image = "notme:0.1.0"` for the `notme-identity` bundle.
- The wire from cloister-router to notme is the workerd service binding (named `NOTME` in cloister-router's bindings, pointing at notme-identity via `serviceBindingProxy` for `/identity/*`).
- For the simple-deploy "docker run cloister-bundled" story, see cloister-side bead `cloister-db99cd` (whether to co-locate notme inside cloister's workerd as a single image — different question; this bead is the separate-container path).

## Refs

- cloister's `~/remotes/art/cloister/cluster.capnp` (the consuming manifest)
- cloister's `~/remotes/art/cloister/docs/deployment/cluster-in-a-pod.md` (operator guide that calls into this)
- cloister-db99cd (sibling: should notme co-locate instead of ship separately?)

## Out of scope

- Co-location with cloister (that's `cloister-db99cd`).
- Multi-tenant scaling of notme (separate concern).
- Anything beyond producing a runnable, tagged image.

title: red-team:trust-root — worker:promote routes 100% production traffic with no gate at all, and ship-prod's "rollback on failure" description was never implemented
description:
red-team:trust-root — filed from adversarial review of PR #70 (origin/goalzero, ADR-018 promotion path).

## Location
- `Taskfile.yml` — `worker:canary`, `worker:promote` (new in PR #70)
- `Taskfile.yml` — `ship-prod` (description edited by PR #70)

## Finding A — the canary/promote tasks have no gate dependency
`worker:promote` is:

```yaml
preconditions:
  - sh: test -n "{{.NEW}}"
cmds:
  - pnpm exec wrangler versions deploy "{{.NEW}}@100%" --yes
```

Its only precondition is that a version id string is non-empty. It does not depend on `worker:check`, `docs:check`, `node:preflight`, `ship-staging`, or `worker:verify`, and it runs no verification afterward. The same is true of `worker:canary`.

Previously the only route to production traffic was `worker:deploy` (via `ship-prod`, which bundles preflight → install → check → docs → deploy → verify) or a bare `task worker:deploy`. PR #70 adds a second route that takes ANY version id in the account's upload history to 100% of production traffic in one command — including a version uploaded before a gate existed, uploaded by a different operator, or uploaded from a branch that never passed staging. Cloudflare retains uploaded versions, so the reachable set is every artifact ever pushed to the account, not just recent ones.

ADR-018's prose ordering (staging → preview → canary → promote) is the only thing sequencing these. Nothing in the Taskfile enforces it, and `ship`'s echo block advertises `task worker:promote NEW=<id>` as a standalone step.

This is a COMMENT rather than a blocker: the operator must type a specific version id, so it is not an accident-shaped hazard, and the artifact plane (tags, cosign, SBOM, npm provenance) is unaffected. But the release story before PR #70 was "the composite task IS the gate," and that property is now gone for the promotion path.

## Finding B — `ship-prod` claims a rollback it does not perform
PR #70 edited this line:

```yaml
ship-prod:
  desc: "Full send: preflight → install → check → docs → deploy → verify (rollback on failure)"
  cmds:
    - task: node:preflight
    - task: worker:install
    - task: worker:check
    - task: docs:check
    - task: worker:deploy
    - task: worker:verify
```

There is no rollback. If `worker:verify` fails, the task exits non-zero with the broken version still serving 100% of traffic. `worker:rollback` exists (`pnpm exec wrangler rollback`) and is never invoked. The claim predates this PR, but PR #70 rewrote the description string and carried it forward, so a reviewer reading the diff sees the assertion re-affirmed.

An operator who trusts the description will not run rollback manually, because they believe it already ran. That is worse than no claim.

## Finding C — `PCT` is unvalidated arithmetic
`worker:canary` computes the fallback share as `{{sub 100 (atoi .PCT)}}`. `PCT=110` yields `-10`; `PCT=abc` yields `atoi` → 0, so `NEW@abc% OLD@100%`. Both are wrangler-rejected rather than silently wrong, so this is cosmetic — noted only so it is not rediscovered.

## On `--yes`
Assessed and cleared. `wrangler versions deploy --yes` skips an interactive confirmation, but the operator has already supplied the exact version ids as explicit `NEW=`/`OLD=` arguments, and the preconditions fail loudly when they are missing. The confirmation prompt was re-stating information the operator just typed; removing it does not remove a decision point. Keeping `--yes` is the right call — a prompt that cannot be answered in CI would push operators toward bypassing the task entirely.

Also correctly handled and worth crediting: the ADR's warning that a version carrying a new `[[migrations]]` entry cannot be split-deployed (DO migrations promote atomically, deleted-class migrations do not roll back). That is the exact failure mode gradual deployments hide, and it is documented at the point of use in the Taskfile comment.

## Detection
Finding A leaves no trace distinguishable from a legitimate promotion. Finding B is silent by construction — the operator's belief is the failure.

## Closing playbook
1. Add `worker:verify` as a follow-on to `worker:promote`, and on failure invoke `worker:rollback` — or, better, promote the OLD id back, since that is the mechanism the ADR already names.
2. Either implement the rollback `ship-prod` advertises, or delete "(rollback on failure)" from the description. Deleting is fine and honest; the current state is not.
3. Gate `worker:promote` on evidence that the named version passed staging — minimally, require a `STAGING_VERIFIED=<version-id>` argument that must equal `NEW`, so promoting an unvetted id is a deliberate typed act rather than the default.

## Confidence
High — all three read directly from the PR #70 diff and the resulting Taskfile.

comments.text:
Re-verified at `41d4f46`. `59042b0` made the canary tasks `ENV`-aware. Findings A and B are unchanged, and the new change adds a third.

**Finding A stands.** `worker:promote` still has exactly one precondition (`test -n "{{.NEW}}"`), no gate dependency, and no follow-on verify.

**Finding B stands.** `ship-prod` still reads `desc: "Full send: preflight → install → check → docs → deploy → verify (rollback on failure)"` with no rollback in the command list.

## Finding D (new, from `59042b0`) — `ENV` defaults to production, and omission is silent

```yaml
vars:
  ENV_FLAG: '{{if .ENV}}--env {{.ENV}}{{end}}'
```

Unset `ENV` yields an empty flag, which wrangler resolves to the **production** environment. Combined with ADR-018's newly-strengthened instruction that "the canary path is **rehearsed on staging with the identical commands** that promote production," the operator now runs the same command string against both environments, distinguished only by an optional variable whose absence means production.

The failure is a dropped `ENV=staging` on what the operator believes is a staging rehearsal:

```
task worker:promote NEW=d0cc333f ENV=staging   # intended
task worker:promote NEW=d0cc333f               # one omission → 100% of PRODUCTION traffic
```

Nothing distinguishes the two at the point of use. There is no confirmation (`--yes`), no echo of the resolved target, and the version ids in ADR-018's own worked example (`d0cc333f`, `f4f2468c`) are staging ids that would be rejected by production — so *that specific* typo fails loudly. But a production id sitting in shell history from an earlier real promotion does not.

This is the cost of the "identical commands" design, which is otherwise the right call — a rehearsal on a different mechanism rehearses nothing. The fix is not to split the commands but to make the target explicit.

**Minimal correction:** require the environment rather than defaulting it — `ENV=production` as a mandatory argument with a precondition, so neither environment is reachable by omission. Failing that, echo the resolved target and version before deploying (`echo "promoting {{.NEW}} to ${ENV:-production}"`) so the operator sees which environment they are about to take to 100%.

Credit where due: `59042b0` also exercised the full canary → rollback cycle on staging and recorded the evidence in ADR-018 (`:220-233`) — version uploaded carrying no traffic, 20/80 split confirmed in `wrangler deployments list`, 12/12 verify green *during* the split, then rollback by promoting the old id. "Rollback is the promote command pointed at the old id, demonstrated, not asserted" is exactly the right standard, and it is now the strongest part of the promotion story. Which is also why Finding B matters more, not less: `ship-prod` claims a rollback that the demonstrated mechanism shows is entirely manual.

title: POST /cert bypasses the CERT_ELIGIBLE_SCOPES allowlist that /cert/passkey enforces — a session can be laundered into a certMint cert
description:
Found by adversarial security review of PR #71 (goal notme-cf288e). PRE-EXISTING — PR #71 does not worsen it, but its new comment at worker/src/cert-exchange.ts blesses the output, so the two files now openly contradict each other.

worker/src/auth/passkey-cert-scopes.ts:39-43 states certMint and authorityManage must NEVER land in a cert, enforced at worker/worker.ts:2252 via CERT_ELIGIBLE_SCOPES={bridgeCert}. The rationale is sound: a cert is long-lived, exportable, usable off-origin, and lacks every property that made granting the browser session acceptable (HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, revocable by clearing a cookie).

worker/src/cert-exchange.ts applies NO such filter. It intersects only against grantedScopes, which is the full admin set on the bootstrap branch and the ENTIRE session's scopes on the session branch. So `POST /cert` with proof:{type:"session"} and scopes:["certMint","authorityManage"] launders an admin's cookie into a 5-minute exportable cert carrying both — exactly what the sibling route's allowlist exists to prevent, one route over.

Inert inside this repo today (AuthService.proxy checks only bridgeCert at worker.ts:424) but NOT inert outside it: gen/go/verify/identity.go:85-90 parses oidScopes into Identity.Scopes for downstream authorization decisions.

Fix: apply the same eligibility filter in cert-exchange.ts, or state explicitly in both files why /cert is exempt and what constrains it instead. The current state — one file forbidding what its sibling freely mints — is the dangerous shape regardless of which way it resolves.

comments.text:
FIXED on goalzero (commit dddf827). Measured before the fix: POST /cert with proof:{type:"session"} from an admin session, requesting ["certMint","authorityManage"], returned 200 with a cert carrying BOTH.

The filter now applies on the CERT branch of cert-exchange.ts via the existing certScopesForSession helper — the same function /cert/passkey uses, so the two routes cannot drift. A request whose scopes are all ineligible gets 403 naming what a certificate may carry, rather than a cert that silently holds less than asked.

DELIBERATELY NOT APPLIED to the token branch below it. The rule belongs to the ARTIFACT, not the route: a certificate is long-lived, exportable and usable off-origin however it was obtained, while that branch mints a short-lived DPoP-bound token with its own controls. Stated at the call site so the asymmetry reads as a decision rather than an oversight.

It also narrows the BOOTSTRAP path, on purpose and worth flagging to anyone reviewing first-boot: that principal still receives bridgeCert+authorityManage+certMint (persisted by notme-92a1b9), but the certificate it walks away with now carries bridgeCert only. Capabilities live on the principal; a cert carries only what is safe to export. This is consistent with the notme-addef9 direction and does not strand a deployer — the admin capability is on the principal, which is the thing that survives.

Three tests, written first and watched fail. The third is the one that matters for regression: it asserts /cert and /cert/passkey now return the SAME scopes for the SAME session, because a rule enforced on one of two routes is the defect, not the rule.

503 unit + 112 real-DO green; staging deployed (462d529f) and `task worker:verify-staging` green end to end.

title: Rate limiter bindings declared only in wrangler.toml.example — TOKEN/CERT/PASSKEY limiters silently no-op in production
description:
Found by adversarial security review of PR #71 (goal notme-cf288e). worker/worker.ts guards every rate-limit call with `if (env.PASSKEY_LIMITER)` / `if (env.TOKEN_LIMITER)` / `if (env.CERT_LIMITER)`, so an absent binding is a SILENT no-op rather than an error.

wrangler.toml.example declares all three [[ratelimits]] blocks (TOKEN_LIMITER 20/min, CERT_LIMITER 10/min, PASSKEY_LIMITER 5/min). The LIVE worker/wrangler.toml (gitignored) declares NONE — verified against the deployed binding list, which shows only SIGNING_AUTHORITY, REVOCATION, CA_BUNDLE_CACHE, ASSETS and the vars. So production and staging currently run with no rate limiting on the passkey registration path, the token endpoint, or cert exchange.

This matters most on /auth/passkey/register/options, which is unauthenticated and is the path that mints bootstrap codes into the Worker logs (see notme-976385's regeneration behavior).

Fix: add the three [[ratelimits]] blocks to the live wrangler.toml and redeploy, then consider whether the `if (env.X_LIMITER)` guards should fail loud in production instead of no-op'ing — a silently absent security control is the defect class here, not the missing config alone. Note the staging env in wrangler.toml.example also omits them and should get them for parity.

title: SAN encoder is short-form-only (≤125 bytes) while cert identity is now variable-length — a long OIDC issuer overflows
description:
Found by adversarial security review of PR #71 (goal notme-cf288e). worker/src/cert-authority.ts:333-340 hand-rolls SubjectAltName with single-byte DER lengths, so the identity URI must stay ≤125 bytes. A length byte >=0x80 reads as long-form, so the mint or the parse errors — availability, not identity confusion. Fails closed.

Before notme-ebc9af the identity's method segment was the constant "passkey" and the URI was a fixed 62 bytes. It is now derived from session.authMethod, so it is variable-length. Measured: passkey 62, invite 61, "oidc:https://auth.notme.bot" 90, "oidc:https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" 111 — only 14 bytes of headroom. A typical Entra issuer with a tenant GUID is ~147 and overflows.

Safe today because verify-proof.ts + packages/contract restrict OIDC issuers to a two-value allowlist, but packages/contract/README.md says deployers MAY extend that list — so this is a trap armed for the first self-hoster with a long issuer.

Fix: emit long-form DER lengths in the SAN encoder (correct fix), or bound identity length at mint time with an explicit error naming the limit (cheap fix). Prefer the former; the encoder is shared.
acceptance_criteria: A test mints a cert with an identity longer than 125 bytes (e.g. a long OIDC issuer) and the resulting cert parses correctly — or fails with an explicit length error naming the limit. cd worker && pnpm exec vitest run passes.

title: notme as identity for entire.io: federation machinery exists, gated on their trusted-issuer list + our ADR-011
description:
What it would take to use notme as identity for entire.io (Git + agent-session checkpointing; entireio/cli is Go/MIT/4.9k stars — core and auth server are closed source).

## What Entire runs today (verified against their code and live endpoints)

- Standard OIDC AS at https://us.auth.entire.io (regional: us/eu/au/in). Discovery advertises authorization_code, device_code, RFC 8693 token-exchange, RFC 7523 jwt-bearer, PKCE S256, and id_token_signing_alg_values_supported [EdDSA, RS256].
- tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens: true (RFC 8705) but NO mtls_endpoint_aliases and NO DPoP.
- CLI flow: browser/device login -> login JWT -> RFC 8693 exchange at the core /oauth/token for repo-scoped tokens (internal/entireclient/httputil/oauth.go, TokenExchangeForm). subject_token_type is hardcoded to access_token.
- ENTIRE_TOKEN env var is the documented CI/workload-identity bypass: "a runner injects a short-lived login or sa-session JWT".
- Core API has /service-accounts/{id}/bindings where a Binding is {providerId, attributeFilter} — the standard OIDC-federation primitive, same shape as GCP WIF and octo-sts trust policies.
- `entire login --server <url>` is a first-class flag; ENTIRE_AUTH_BASE_URL was retired in favour of it.

## Blocker on their side

https://entire.io/.well-known/entire-api.json publishes a FIXED trusted_issuers list: the four *.auth.entire.io regional servers, nothing else. /api/v1/oidc-providers is GET-only (no POST) and returns 401. No self-service way to register an external issuer, and the CLI has no command touching it, so it is console/admin-side.

The federation machinery Entire would need in order to accept notme already exists and is already wired. The only missing piece is an entry in a server-side list we cannot write. That makes this a small, well-shaped ask of them rather than an architecture change.

## Blocker on our side

ADR-013 deliberately keeps authorization_endpoint and code_challenge_methods_supported in FORBIDDEN_METADATA_FIELDS because publishing them advertises "notme is an OAuth AS you can integrate with" — and there is still no client registry and no consent screen behind it. That is ADR-011 (Proposed, unimplemented). Third-party federation with Entire is precisely the case ADR-013 was withholding those fields to prevent, so ADR-011 is a hard prerequisite for the clean path.

## Compatibility that already lines up

- notme signs EdDSA/Ed25519; Entire accepts EdDSA id_tokens.
- notme serves /.well-known/openid-configuration and /.well-known/jwks.json live — exactly what their jwks_uris map consumes.
- Issuer https://auth.notme.bot is stable and HTTPS.
- notme already mints from GHA OIDC, which is the identity their CI path wants.

## Options, cheapest first

1. Custodian, not issuer (needs no cooperation). notme fronts the Entire credential: GHA OIDC -> notme cert -> notme vends a short-lived Entire login JWT it holds. Entire sees a normal Entire token. HONEST CAVEAT: this moves the secret into notme rather than eliminating it — you still bootstrap from an Entire-issued refresh/sa token. Weaker than it looks. Ties to notme-724300 (secretless proxy).
2. Ask them to add https://auth.notme.bot as an OIDC provider, then bind a service account with an attributeFilter. Requires ADR-011 first. This is the real integration and uses only machinery they already ship.
3. Differentiated angle. Their CI tokens are bearer tokens; they advertise mTLS binding but ship no mtls_endpoint_aliases and no DPoP. notme does cert identity + RFC 9449 DPoP. This is where notme is additive rather than duplicative, and the strongest thing to lead with when talking to them.

## Footgun worth raising with them

CreateBindingInputBody.attributeFilter is documented as "Exact-match key/value map; empty filter matches any token." An empty filter means any identity from that issuer can assume the service account — the misconfiguration class behind real GCP Workload Identity Federation breaches. Fail-closed (require a non-empty filter) would be the safer default.

## Already banked

Fixed while doing this assessment: FORBIDDEN_METADATA_FIELDS comments claimed "PKCE is unimplemented" (ADR-013 shipped S256) and had never been narrowed the way ADR-013 said they would be. Branch notme-as-metadata-pkce-comment.
acceptance_criteria: Decision recorded on which of the three integration options to pursue, and (if option 2) a concrete ask sent to Entire. Superseded if Entire ships self-service OIDC provider registration.

title: Invites survive a passkey reset and have no TTL ceiling — an authorityManage invite is an uncounted way in
description:
Found by adversarial security review of PR #71 (goal notme-cf288e), round 2. Two related gaps in the "can anyone authenticate?" predicate (#hasAuthenticator in worker/src/signing-authority.ts), both narrower than the H1 defect already fixed, neither blocking that PR.

1. resetPasskeyData wipes passkey_* and (as of PR #71) rotates the session secret, but does NOT touch the `invites` table. redeemInvite (worker/src/auth/principals.ts:216-231) checks only redeemed_at and expires_at, so an outstanding invite outlives any reset and remains a way in that #hasAuthenticator does not count.

2. The invite TTL is caller-supplied with NO upper bound: worker/worker.ts:1887 passes `body.ttl ?? 3600` straight through, and neither createInviteToken (signing-authority.ts) nor createInvite (principals.ts:203-214) clamps it. An authorityManage invite can therefore be minted with an arbitrarily long life.

Fix options: revoke or expire outstanding invites in resetPasskeyData (making "reset" total, consistent with the session-secret rotation already added); clamp invite TTL to a documented ceiling; and/or count unredeemed unexpired invites in #hasAuthenticator. The first two are preferable — the predicate is more honest when "reset" genuinely leaves nobody able to authenticate.

Related gap from the same review, worth handling together: a principal that joined via invite and never registered a passkey nor linked an OIDC identity is invisible to #hasAuthenticator (the federated link at worker.ts:1933-1945 is best-effort inside a try/catch that swallows failure). Contrived today — the FIRST admin must come from passkey registration or /cert — but it is the same error class with a different population.

comments.text:
IMPORTANT REACHABILITY FINDING from the dataflow integration review — this gap is NOT currently reachable, and the reason is load-bearing enough to record here rather than leave implicit.

resetPasskeyData is the ONLY code path anywhere in the worker that deletes credentials. There is no `DELETE FROM federated_identities`, no `DELETE FROM principals`, and no `DELETE FROM invites` in the codebase at all. So reaching the dangerous state — "no authenticator counted, but an outstanding authorityManage invite is still redeemable" — requires losing your credential, which requires resetPasskeyData, which requires consuming a bootstrap code, which requires already having no authenticator. The transition is CIRCULAR and cannot be entered.

That means this bead is safe today, contingent on a fact nobody had written down: that credential removal has exactly one entrance. It becomes a live hole the moment anyone adds a second credential-removal path — an admin "revoke device" route, a GDPR delete, a principal-deletion API. Whoever adds one must either revoke outstanding invites in the same operation or make #hasAuthenticator count them.

This does not lower the bead's priority, it sharpens the fix: the TTL ceiling half (invite TTL is caller-supplied with no upper bound, worker.ts:1887 → `body.ttl ?? 3600` unclamped) is independently worth doing, and the invite-revocation-on-reset half is what keeps the circularity from mattering when it inevitably breaks.

Suggest the guard land as a comment at the top of resetPasskeyData naming it the sole credential-removal path, so the next person to add one sees the constraint at the site they would violate.

rsry-mcp

comments.text:
This is more urgent than "replace a placeholder", and the PEN is not the blocking part.

## The live defect

notme and cloister both use `1.3.6.1.4.1.99999` and assign **conflicting meanings to the same OIDs**:

| OID | notme (`cert-authority.ts:60-74`) | cloister (`interlace-spec/0.1.0/wire/cert-extensions.md`) |
|---|---|---|
| `.1.4` | CA epoch | `interlace-epoch` INTEGER — agrees |
| `.1.5` | authMethod | `interlace-peer` UTF8String — **collides** |
| `.1.6` | `SHA-256(P-256 SPKI \|\| Ed25519 SPKI)` binary | `interlace-scope` UTF8String — **collides** |

A notme cert fed to cloister's Interlace verifier reads an authMethod string as a peer fingerprint and a binary hash as a UTF-8 scope. cloister fails closed when those are absent or malformed (`lease-middleware.ts:471`), and its profile rejects unknown critical extensions — which notme's signing cert carries (BasicConstraints, KeyUsage, SAN).

Found via a codex adversarial review of the cloister dev-bootstrap problem statement; verified directly in both trees. This is why notme cannot currently mint a cloister lease identity — the blocker was never authorization, it is the certificate profile.

## Registry facts (checked 2026-08-05)

- Registration is **free** and first-come-first-served under RFC 9371.
- Apply at https://www.iana.org/assignments/enterprise-numbers/assignment/apply/ — requires only organization/individual name, contact name, contact email.
- IANA: "you should receive an assignment within seven (7) days" absent follow-up questions.
- `99999` is currently **unassigned**, but the highest assigned PEN in the registry is **66445**. The placeholder is borrowed, not safe indefinitely.

## Order of work — the numeric swap is last, not first

1. **Deconflict the arc layout. Blocking, free, do first.** Swapping `99999` for a real PEN does nothing on its own: `.1.5` would still mean two things. Proposed split so projects cannot collide:
   - `<PEN>.1.*` — Interlace wire (epoch, peer, scope). cloister's `interlace-spec/0.1.0` is the versioned normative document and its verifier enforces it, so Interlace owns this subtree.
   - `<PEN>.2.*` — notme authority extensions (subject, issuance time, scopes, authMethod, peer-binding).

   This is what makes a notme-minted Interlace lease cert expressible at all — one cert can then carry both sets without either verifier misreading the other's fields.

2. **Apply for ONE PEN for the organization**, not one per repo. A PEN is per-enterprise; the subtree is then ours to allocate.

3. **Collapse the hardcoded sites first.** 9 files in each repo contain the literal arc. notme is close — `cert-authority.ts` has a single `OID_PEN` and derives the rest; the other hits are docs. cloister spreads it across `interlace-spec`, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/adr/0007`, and two tests. One constant per repo turns the eventual swap into 2 edits.

4. **Keep a sub-arc registry** — a single file recording every assignment under the PEN. An unmanaged namespace collides silently; this one did, and it surfaced only because an external reviewer read both trees at once.

## Cross-links

- `notme-ebc9af` — the `/cert/passkey` authMethod provenance defect, same certificate path.
- cloister-side: the dev-bootstrap thread (`cloister-f2338f`) whose stated ask cannot be satisfied until item 1 lands.

When WIMSE finalizes, alignment is a media type + header name change, not an architecture change.\n\nDowngrading from P2 to P3. The bridge cert path (mTLS) is the primary mechanism. title: Replace keyIdFromSpki with the canonical BLAKE3 kid; epoch-rotate JWKS; keep opaque-match
description:
notme currently derives its JWK `kid` via `keyIdFromSpki` (RFC-7638-ish truncated SHA-256 over SPKI DER — worker/src/key-id.ts, per worker/README.md:182). Switch to the canonical derivation defined by signet (BLAKE3 over the raw Ed25519 public key, 128-bit) so an LLO signed head's signerKid and a cloister verifier resolve against notme's JWKS.

Scope:
1. Replace keyIdFromSpki with the canonical kid. Publish it in both `/.well-known/jwks.json` (keys[].kid) AND the JWT header kid — they must move together.
2. Because kid is opaque-matched by consumers (worker.js:37085 `keys.find(k => k.kid === header.kid)`), the change is safe as a key-rotation/epoch event: bump the epoch so caches (1hr TTL) refresh. No external consumer recomputes the kid (Cloudflare Access is upstream of notme, not a downstream kid consumer — verified 2026-07-21).
3. Add a test gating notme's kid against signet's pinned vector fixture.

Note: `keyIdFromSpki` may still be needed anywhere an X.509 SubjectKeyId is expected — do not delete it blindly; scope its remaining callers first. This bead is about the PROTOCOL kid (JWKS/JWT), not the cert SubjectKeyId.

Close condition: `cd ~/remotes/art/notme && <the JS test runner, e.g. pnpm -C worker test>` green including the new vector-conformance test.
