title: Delegation chain as correlation key — one prefix-closed identifier for "what happened under X" and "what falls when X is revoked"
description:
DESIRED OUTCOME: align records the way one aligns journalctl / syslog / nginx / dmesg — pick something that happened, see everything that happened under it — and have REVOCATION follow a matching closure, working offline and at the edge.

NOTE: this description was REWRITTEN 2026-08-06 after a formal review falsified the original proposal. The original keyed everything on certificate serials and claimed ONE identifier could serve both correlation and revocation. Both were wrong; see "what was wrong" below. The corrected shape is IMPLEMENTED at `worker/src/auth/correlation-key.ts` with tests.

── THE SHAPE ──
    <principal>                   everything that principal ever did
    <principal>/<bridge>          one machine session
    <principal>/<bridge>/<task>   one task

PRINCIPAL, not a root key id — it is the level a human asks questions about, and it survives CA rotation.
BINDING, not a certificate serial. `mintBridgeCertPair` issues TWO certs with two independently random serials, so no single serial names "the bridge"; it names half of one. The pair already has an identifier: `binding = SHA-256(P-256 SPKI || Ed25519 SPKI)`, returned by that function and carried at OID_PEER_BINDING. The keypairs are ephemeral, so this identifies a machine SESSION — the right granularity for the middle level.
TASK, opaque. notme does not decide what upstream calls a unit of work.

── WHAT WAS WRONG WITH THE ORIGINAL PROPOSAL ──
1. SERIALS NAME CERTIFICATE INSTANCES, NOT IDENTITIES. On renewal the subtree FORKS: "everything under this machine" silently splits across serials. Revocation wants instance precision; correlation wants principal stability. One string cannot carry both equivalence classes.
2. THE CIDR ANALOGY WAS THE COUNTEREXAMPLE, NOT THE SUPPORT. Routing and firewalling share prefixes because both read the SAME CURRENT MAPPING. Historical logs keyed by IP are the textbook "IP ≠ identity" forensic ambiguity — exactly the current-state-versus-history split the proposal papered over.
3. INCOMPATIBLE STORE LIFECYCLES. Revocation must be mutable and pruned to keep the hot auth path bounded; correlation must be append-only. One store gives either deleted history or an unbounded auth check.
4. REVOCATION NEEDS NO KEY AT ALL. Revoking a bridge cert fails every task cert beneath it BY ISSUER — intrinsic X.509 path validation. A prefix key would be an INDEX for edge lookups, never the mechanism. The original overstated it.

So: TWO keys, TWO stores. This bead is now only the CORRELATION half.

── A DEFECT THE REVIEW DID NOT COVER, FOUND WHILE IMPLEMENTING ──
`<principal>/<bridge>/<task>` is not implementable as written. The principal is a WIMSE URI that ALREADY CONTAINS SLASHES (`wimse://notme.bot/passkey/<uuid>`), so joining raw produces two silent defects, both of which OVER-MATCH — and for a correlation key over-matching means attributing one principal's activity to another:

  PHANTOM LEVELS — the principal's own slashes read as level boundaries, so a prefix aimed at the bridge level lands inside the principal.
  STRING-PREFIX IS NOT SEGMENT-PREFIX — "a/b" is a string prefix of "a/bb", so a query for `wimse://x/a` also matches `wimse://x/ab`.

Both are fixed by percent-encoding each segment and TERMINATING every key and prefix with the delimiter, so a match can only land on a boundary. A plain `startsWith` — or a KV `list({prefix})` at the edge — is then exact with no parsing on the hot path. Same hazard as the identity-URI parsing note in gen/go/verify/identity.go; there the answer was a comment telling consumers not to parse, but here the structure IS the point, so the encoding must make parsing safe rather than forbid it.

── THE PROPERTY THAT MAKES IT TRUSTWORTHY ──
W3C Trace Context (`traceparent`) is the existing answer to correlation and is COMPLETELY UNAUTHENTICATED — any process writes any trace id, so today one can correlate but not ATTRIBUTE.

journald is the better model and notme is already shaped for it. `_SYSTEMD_UNIT` is trustworthy because JOURNALD attaches it; a process cannot lie about its own unit because it never writes that field. The same chokepoint exists here: ADR-009 leaves the agent Worker no `globalOutbound`, so it cannot `fetch()` at all, and ADR-007's proxy holds the credential and performs every outbound request. THE PROXY IS JOURNALD — it can stamp the key with no path around it. That the key is PRINCIPAL-shaped rather than serial-shaped strengthens this, since the proxy knows the principal from the cert it holds.

── WHAT REMAINS ──
1. WIRE IT INTO THE RECORD. `worker/src/receipts/commitment.ts` is master-key signed and canonical-CBOR encoded, but its schema is REQUEST-shaped: `nonce`, `request_hash`, `body_hash`, `headers_hash`, `timestamp_ms`. It carries no subject and no granter, so a receipt proves a request happened and CANNOT say who was acting under whose delegation. Adding the key is a COORDINATED change — the schema is versioned and cloister consumes it (RECEIPTS.md §2.1).
2. STAMP IT IN THE PROXY (`proxy/src/main.rs`), which is where the unforgeability argument is actually cashed.
3. The `<task>` level has no producer until hop 2 exists (notme-600df1).

── WHY THIS IS NOT MERELY OBSERVABILITY ──
Revocation by subtree works via issuer chaining, but ENUMERATING what a revocation affected — "what did this machine touch before we cut it" — is an incident-response question that only the correlation record can answer. The two are separate mechanisms serving one investigation.

BLOCKED ON, for the task level only: notme-600df1.
RELATED: notme-77a024 (revocation unit), notme-907299 (issuance transparency), notme-acc822 (the chain constraints that make the tree well-formed).
PRIOR ART: macaroons and Biscuit make the attenuation chain the audit trail and verify offline.

comments.text:
CORRECTION AFTER FORMAL REVIEW (theoretical-foundations-analyst, 2026-08-06). The central claim of this bead — that ONE prefix-closed identifier serves both correlation and revocation — is UNSOUND. Two structures that look alike were collapsed. The bead's underlying goal survives; the proposed mechanism does not.

── DEFECT 1: INSTANCE VERSUS PRINCIPAL GRANULARITY ──
Serial numbers name CERTIFICATE INSTANCES, not identities. When a bridge cert renews — same machine, new serial — the correlation subtree FORKS: "everything that happened under this machine" now spans multiple `<bridge-serial>` prefixes. Same again at `<root-kid>` on rotation, which is exactly why the epoch extension exists.

The two uses want opposite equivalence classes. Revocation wants INSTANCE precision: revoke this certificate, not this principal forever. Correlation wants PRINCIPAL stability: "what happened during X" means the machine, across renewals. One string cannot carry both.

── DEFECT 2: MY CIDR ANALOGY WAS THE COUNTEREXAMPLE, NOT THE SUPPORT ──
Routing and firewalling share prefixes because both consume the SAME CURRENT MAPPING. Historical logs keyed by IP are the classic forensic ambiguity — "IP ≠ identity" the moment addresses are reassigned. So CIDR demonstrates that a prefix scheme serves current-state uses well and HISTORICAL CORRELATION BADLY, which is precisely the split the bead papered over.

── DEFECT 3: THE IDENTIFIER NAMES HALF A DELEGATION ──
Verified in `cert-authority.ts:346-355`: `mintBridgeCertPair` issues TWO certificates (mTLS + signing) with two independently random serials. "The bridge" is two nodes, so `<bridge-serial>` is ambiguous by construction. The correct bridge-node identifier already exists in the cert format: `OID_PEER_BINDING` = SHA-256(P-256 SPKI || Ed25519 SPKI) at cert-authority.ts:73. That hash, not either serial.

── DEFECT 4: INCOMPATIBLE STORE LIFECYCLES ──
The revocation store must be MUTABLE AND PRUNED — expired entries removed to keep the hot auth path bounded. The correlation store must be APPEND-ONLY AND IMMUTABLE. Unify them behind one key and you get one of two classic bugs: pruning revocations deletes history, or retaining history bloats every auth check.

── ALSO WORTH KNOWING: SUBTREE REVOCATION NEEDS NO IDENTIFIER AT ALL ──
Revoke the bridge cert and every task cert under it fails path validation because its ISSUER is revoked. That is intrinsic X.509 behaviour. The prefix key would be an INDEX — useful for a KV prefix-match check at the edge — not the revocation mechanism. The bead overstated it as the mechanism.

── THE REPAIR: TWO KEYS, TWO STORES ──
  CORRELATION: `<principal-uri>/<peer-binding>/<task-id>` — WIMSE URI at the top so it is STABLE ACROSS ROTATION. Append-only.
  REVOCATION:  serial-keyed, pruned current-state — or simply lean on chain validation and revoke the intermediate.

Prefix-closure of the CHAIN is real and useful: it licenses subtree semantics in each store SEPARATELY. What it does not license is one identifier serving both.

── WHAT SURVIVES UNCHANGED ──
Everything about WHY this matters. The receipt schema is still request-shaped and still carries no granter (`receipts/commitment.ts` — nonce, request_hash, body_hash, headers_hash, timestamp_ms), so a receipt still cannot say who was acting under whose delegation. Revocation without enumeration is still unenforceable. The journald argument is untouched and is the strongest part: ADR-009 leaves the agent no `globalOutbound` and ADR-007's proxy makes every outbound request, so the proxy can stamp an unforgeable correlation key the agent cannot set — which is what distinguishes this from `traceparent`. That the key should be principal-shaped rather than serial-shaped makes the stamping argument stronger, not weaker.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
FILED TO CLOISTER AS cloister-c10ff2, since they own the Interlace spec and notme cannot extend it by deploying.

THE HONEST STATE OF THE FIELD: notme will SIGN a nine-key commitment, and no verifier is obliged to accept one. RECEIPTS.md §2.1 defines exactly eight keys, so a conformant P implementing the strict reading rejects it. The field is therefore INERT END-TO-END until cloister decides. That is intended rather than unfortunate — the alternative is notme widening another repo's wire format unilaterally, and §11 of their own spec states the principle ("extensions require SEP amendment, not deploy-time changes", said there of the header allowlist).

A FINDING WORTH MORE THAN THE PROPOSAL, surfaced while checking whether a nine-key commitment would even be rejected. §2.2.1 states two different strictnesses and only one is explicit:

  step 2 (ENVELOPE):   "reject if not a valid map with exactly the keys {commitment, signature}"
  step 3 (COMMITMENT): "Parse commitment as CBOR with the keys named in §2.1"

Step 2 says EXACTLY; step 3 does not. So whether a conformant verifier must reject an unrecognised extra key inside the commitment is UNDEFINED, and two conformant implementations can legitimately differ — one rejecting, one ignoring the extra field and verifying the rest. An implementation that ignores unknown keys is accepting signed-but-unspecified data: bytes inside the signature its verifier does not interpret and something downstream might. One that rejects makes every future field a hard fork. Both defensible; the spec has to pick, and step 3 should say it in step 2's words.

notme implements the STRICT reading, chosen independently before the ambiguity was noticed. If cloister's verifier implements the permissive one, the two have been diverging silently — which is the actual risk here, and it exists whether or not `delegation` is ever adopted.

ALSO FLAGGED TO THEM: `CommitmentErrorCode` gained DELEGATION_MISMATCH. That union is a wire contract cloister branches on exhaustively and fails closed on anything unrecognised, so adding a code is safe rather than breaking — but a switch wanting the specific arm now has one to add. Not retryable; RETRYABLE_CODES still contains only EPOCH_MISMATCH.

FOUR QUESTIONS PUT TO THEM: resolve step 3's strictness (needed regardless); adopt or decline the field; if adopted, optional-forever or required at a future version; and whether the audit/disclosure path verifies it or treats it as opaque payload. Declining is a real answer — notme's implementation is inert without them and can be removed.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
THE SATISFACTION COUNTERPART — recorded here because it uses the same signing surface, and folded into ADR-019 rather than a new ADR because it needs no new credential type.

This bead's `delegation` field answers WHO WAS ACTING UNDER WHOSE DELEGATION. It does not and cannot answer WHETHER THE WORK IS DONE. Those are the attribution and satisfaction halves of the same record.

FIVE CLAIMS HIDE BEHIND "done", and collapsing any two is a defect:
  delegation   — you may attempt this        (grantor,        directive)
  promise      — you undertake this task     (actor,          commissive)
  submission   — the work is finished        (actor,          commissive)
  verification — evidence meets the predicate (verifier,      assertive)
  acceptance   — it is done                  (task authority, DECLARATIVE)

An agent's `end_turn`, clean exit, or "done" message is only SUBMISSION. Only an authority can perform a declarative, which is why acceptance cannot be self-signed — the same reasoning APAS already applies to orchestrator self-attestation. Promise Theory gives the general form: an agent can promise its own behaviour and never impose an obligation on another, so the verifier makes its own separate promise to evaluate.

ACCEPTANCE IS A GRANT, not a new object: `scopes: ["accept:<taskHash>"]`, inheriting grant_id, parent_grant_id, expiry and delegable from ADR-019 D3. That closes a recursion a standalone `verifierPolicy` field leaves open — WHO AUTHORISED THE VERIFIER — and makes "who may accept" revocable by the same mechanism as everything else.

THREE CONSTRAINTS, each easy to get wrong:
1. THE VERIFIER MUST SIT OUTSIDE THE ACTOR'S BLAST RADIUS. "CI passed against the commit digest" looks independent and frequently is not: CI is an agent executing configuration from the repository under test. If the workflow definition is within the actor's write scope, CI is self-attestation with extra steps — the same defect class as this repo's structurally-always-empty workflow outputs and the action that pinned itself. It is checkable, so make it a stated precondition.
2. A CLOSE CONDITION IS EITHER MACHINE-EVALUABLE OR HUMAN-JUDGED, and must declare which. Hashing a predicate commits to its WORDING; it does not make it evaluable. Most interesting conditions are human judgement in a machine-checkable costume, and the distinction must be forced at authoring time.
3. LIVENESS PREDICATES ARE NOT SETTLED BY A SIGNATURE. "SLO held 24h" is continuously falsifiable, so acceptance carries a validity window and is itself a lease — submitted→verified→accepted stops being monotonic. Also missing from every version of this so far: THERE IS NO REJECTION PATH. Verification fails, and then what? Unbounded retry against a verifier is a brute-force oracle in some settings.

ENFORCEMENT IS A SHORT LEASE, NEVER "valid until done". A credential whose lifetime is defined by task state requires every verifier to know that state — the identical error to assuming a recorded revocation invalidates a chain someone already holds (ADR-019 Consequences). Minutes-long credentials, a controller renewing only while the task is active, acceptance stops renewal. Immediate termination still needs online revocation or an introspecting tool boundary.

WHERE IT LIVES, and this is the small part: an acceptance attestation is structurally a receipt — a signed statement about an event with derived-not-received fields. `ReceiptSigner` already has the master key, canonical CBOR, and the validate-then-sign discipline refusing caller-supplied bytes. Same surface, second field.

BEFORE ANY OF IT IS BUILT: in-toto LAYOUTS already express "these steps, these expected materials and products, and these functionary keys may sign each step" — a task contract plus verifier policy in one signed artifact, with in-toto-verify as the evaluator, CNCF and already in the SLSA ecosystem. So the question is not what object is missing but WHAT APAS ADDS THAT A LAYOUT DOES NOT — plausibly the delegation chain, the represented principal, and an actor that was itself delegated to mid-execution, none of which in-toto's functionary model covers. Extending it beats a parallel format. Recorded as ADR-019 open question 6.

title: P-256 PoP double-hashes: WebCrypto ECDSA verify is handed the digest, not the pre-image
description:
Found by signet's v0.3.0-rc.2 release run against the freshly deployed production Worker (run 31065683262, 2026-08-06T02:29Z). This is a SECOND bug in the same handler, which the first one was masking: with the stale deploy the import threw before verify could run, so nobody could observe that verify would also fail. Deploying version 39e0b216 fixed the import and revealed this.

The error changed, which is the evidence the deploy worked:
  rc.1 (stale): "P-256 proof verification error: Requested algorithm \"ECDSA\" does not match this CryptoKey's algorithm \"Ed25519\"" — import threw
  rc.2 (deployed): "P-256 proof-of-possession failed" — import fine, verify RAN and returned false

ROOT CAUSE — a double hash, reproduced rather than reasoned about.

worker/worker.ts computes bindingPayload = SHA-256(bindingInput), then calls:
  crypto.subtle.verify({name:"ECDSA", hash:"SHA-256"}, mtlsPubKey, proofBytes, bindingPayload)

WebCrypto's ECDSA verify HASHES ITS data ARGUMENT. Passing bindingPayload therefore verifies the signature against SHA-256(SHA-256(bindingInput)).

signet signs the other thing: Go's ecdsa.Sign(rand, key, binding) treats its input as an already-computed digest, so cmd/sigstore-kms-signet/enroll.go:131 produces a signature over SHA-256(bindingInput) — one hash, not two.

REPRODUCTION (Go generates a signet-shaped proof; Node's WebCrypto verifies it exactly as the Worker does):
  verify(data = binding digest)    [as deployed]  : false
  verify(data = binding pre-image) [proposed fix] : true

WHY ONLY THE P-256 PROOF. The Ed25519 proof on the same request succeeds, because WebCrypto Ed25519 is PureEdDSA and does not pre-hash — both sides operate on `binding` directly and agree. Only the ECDSA path has an implicit hash on the verifier side, so only it diverges. That asymmetry is exactly what makes this easy to miss when reading the two blocks side by side: they look symmetric and are not.

FIX: pass the PRE-IMAGE to the ECDSA verify — bindingInput, not bindingPayload — and let WebCrypto apply the single hash. One argument. No signet change is needed or wanted; signet's construction is the conventional one for Go ECDSA.

Suggested guard so this cannot regress silently: a test that verifies a KNOWN-GOOD fixture proof generated by a Go signer, rather than by the Worker's own signing code. A round-trip test written entirely in WebCrypto would pass under both the broken and fixed versions, because it would double-hash consistently on both sides — the same shape of trap as the JWKS-kid signal you hit while validating the deploy.

comments.text:
FIXED AND DEPLOYED. Production is version 91b54069 at 100%, worker:verify 13/13 green. Signet can cut v0.3.0-rc.3 — the Go signer path works now, and the pinned action was NOT broken in the process (see the migration window below).

ROOT CAUSE, confirmed empirically rather than argued. `crypto.subtle.verify({name:"ECDSA", hash:"SHA-256"}, …)` applies SHA-256 to whatever it is handed, and every site handed it `bindingPayload = SHA-256(bindingInput)`. The verified message was therefore hashed TWICE. Go's `ecdsa.Sign(rand, priv, digest)` applies none, so a conformant Go signer produces one hash and could never match. A characterization test asserts this directly — the digest FAILS and the pre-image VERIFIES against the same signature — so the diagnosis is falsifiable, not merely plausible.

WHY IT SURVIVED, and the reason the fixture is what it is: notme's own action signed the same doubled way, so signer and verifier were consistently wrong and a round trip between them passed. That is a fixed point, not a conformance check — the identical failure already recorded for the receipt encoder, whose fixtures were built with the encoder under test. So the regression fixture is STATIC AND FOREIGN: generated once by node:crypto (which hashes exactly once, like Go) and pasted in. Nothing in this repo can regenerate it, so a change that reintroduces double-hashing on BOTH sides cannot make it pass again. That satisfies the acceptance criterion literally.

SCOPE WAS LARGER THAN TWO CALL SITES. Three handlers — /cert/gha, /cert, /cert/passkey — each carried their own inline copy: two verify calls wrapped in try/catch, six blocks across two files. That duplication is why the convention could drift on all of them at once without any single change looking wrong. They now share one verifier, `worker/src/auth/pop.ts`. Ed25519 does not double-hash but is held to the SAME rule deliberately: two proofs in one request covering different bytes is a trap that only ever surfaces as an opaque 401.

── THE PART THAT CHANGED THE PLAN: A CLEAN CUT WAS NOT AVAILABLE ──
The signer and verifier ship from different places. The Worker deploys from this repo; `.github/workflows/gha-identity.yml:137` pins `agentic-research/notme/action` at a COMMIT SHA. Deploying the corrected verifier alone breaks that pinned action. Bumping the pin alone breaks it against the old verifier. They can only cross together — and the pin bump cannot land before the goalzero→main merge, so a flag day meant either a broken window or holding signet's release behind an unrelated merge gate.

So the verifier accepts BOTH encodings for now and REPORTS WHICH ONE MATCHED (`binding: "pre-image" | "digest"`). The reporting is the load-bearing half: without it a legacy caller is indistinguishable from a fixed one and the transitional branch could never be safely removed. Safe because both encodings are deterministic functions of the same two public keys proved by the same private keys — accepting either lets a caller assert nothing it could not already assert with the other, and neither message is meaningful input to any other verifier here. The digest is computed lazily, so a conformant caller never pays for the legacy path.

REMOVAL IS TRACKED ON THIS BEAD, not a TODO: delete `ACCEPT_LEGACY_DIGEST_BINDING` and the second attempt once the action pin is bumped past 0d2312f and nothing reports `binding: "digest"`.

EXISTING TESTS CAUGHT THE CONTRACT CHANGE — 7 DO tests failed with 401 because their helpers built proofs the old way, which is the correct behaviour for a wire-format change and the reason to be confident the change is real. Updated to sign the pre-image. Full suites: 508 unit + 120 DO passing.

Commits: 0d2312f (fix + shared verifier + action in lockstep), plus the migration window.

comments.text:
POSITIVE EVIDENCE NOW EXISTS. Signet's objection was correct and is worth quoting because it identified a real gap, not a misunderstanding:

  "notme's double-hash fix still isn't in their origin/main. Their deploys are
   manual so the tree doesn't settle what's deployed — but there's no positive
   evidence it's fixed either."

BOTH HALVES WERE ACCURATE. The fix is on `goalzero`, which is 92 commits ahead of `origin/main` and merges once — so the tree genuinely did not settle the question. And there was no positive evidence: `/health` returned the string `ok`, nothing else served was derived from the build, and `worker:verify` never touches a PoP path. I also confirmed there is no unauthenticated probe that reaches the verifier — in POST /cert the session check runs BEFORE verifyPopProofs, so an outside caller cannot exercise it. Signet was right that asking was the only option.

WHAT EXISTS NOW:

  $ curl -s https://auth.notme.bot/.well-known/version
  {"commit":"c0f80012e6e18bef7d0b08efc928b36f373ec015","stamped":true}

Stable across repeated reads, no-store, unauthenticated, ACAO *. `0d2312f` — the PoP pre-image fix — is an ancestor of that commit, verified with `git merge-base --is-ancestor`. So the deployed build provably contains the fix, and anyone can check it themselves rather than taking notme's word.

STILL TRUE, and unchanged: the fix is NOT in origin/main. That is the branch model (feature → goalzero → one PR → main), not an oversight, and it will remain true until the release merge. Signet should pin their expectations to the DEPLOYED commit, which is now readable, rather than to origin/main.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT PROVE: that a real GHA enrollment succeeds end to end. That still requires an OIDC token notme cannot mint for its own endpoint, so signet's rc.3 run remains the only evidence for clause 1 of notme-718ac0. What changed is that they can now confirm WHICH BUILD they are testing against before spending a tag on it — which was the actual blocker in their message.

The version endpoint is also the discriminator notme-9f2f79 needed; details there.

title: ADR-010's hard-cutover decision is justified by a fail-closed property no request path exercises (isBundleStale has no production caller)
description:
Documentation-honesty audit finding (Goal Zero criterion A), notme-bed754. ADR-010 is `Accepted` (2026-05-09).

## The claim

`docs/design/010-cross-language-canonical-encoding.md:110`, the decision paragraph choosing hard-cutover (B) over dual-encode (A):

> **Decision (2026-05-10): (B) hard-cutover.** notme is currently pre-production; no persistent JSON-canonical signed bundles in any production KV need preserving. The 4-minute alarm cycle bounds the unverifiable-bundle window during deploy; **revocation checks fail closed during that window (per `revocation.ts::isBundleStale`)**, which is the same fail-closed behavior they'd take on any bundle staleness anyway.

The same section (:107) sets up the alternative it rejects: strategy (A) is "Conservative; appropriate for production deployments with persistent signed bundles to preserve."

## What is actually true

`isBundleStale` has exactly one caller anywhere: `checkRevocation` in the same file. And `checkRevocation` has **no production caller at all** — `worker.ts` never imports `src/revocation.ts` (it only re-exports the `RevocationAuthority` class so wrangler can bind the DO) and never references `env.REVOCATION`. Verified three ways because grep under-reports here: `rg`, `git grep`, and a `find … -exec grep -l` sweep over every `.ts`/`.rs`/`.go` outside node_modules — all three return only `revocation.ts`, `revocation.do.test.ts`, `pool-test-env.d.ts` and the vitest workers config.

So during the 4-minute window the decision reasons about, nothing performs a revocation check at all — neither fail-closed nor fail-open. The safety property the decision leans on is not weaker than described; it is not exercised. The choice between (A) and (B) may still have been correct on its other grounds (pre-production, no persistent bundles), but one of the two stated grounds is unsupported.

Two further details worth recording while correcting this:

1. Even in the hypothetical wired world, `checkRevocation` **fails open** when KV holds no bundle at all — pinned by `revocation.do.test.ts:198` *"fails open when no bundle in KV (bootstrap)"*. The blanket "fail closed on any bundle staleness" reading is true for a present-but-stale bundle and false for an absent one.
2. `BUNDLE_MAX_AGE_MS` (5 min) and `BUNDLE_REFRESH_MS` (4 min) are still correctly ordered (`src/signing-authority.ts:88` documents the dependency), so the timing half of the argument holds.

## Why it is worth a correction rather than a shrug

This is the same defect class GOAL-ZERO-STATUS §7 names — "an artifact asserting a property of its own provenance that nothing verified" — applied to a migration-risk argument. ADR-010's whole subject is a docstring that claimed a guarantee (`Cap'n Proto's deterministic binary format guarantees this`) that nothing delivered; the ADR correcting it then made a structurally identical move in its own decision paragraph. A future reader choosing (A) vs (B) for a *production* deployment with persistent bundles — which the ADR explicitly anticipates at :112 — would be reasoning from a mitigation that does not exist.

The rest of ADR-010 is unusually honest and should be left alone: the fixture-suite status note at :127-138 is precise about what shipped on which side and names the two beads that have not (`signet-0454a2`, `ley-line-open-0466c0`), and the "Honest docstrings" consequence is exactly right.

## How verified

Read ADR-010 in full. `git grep -n "checkRevocation\|isBundleStale" -- .` and `rg -n "isBundleStale\|BUNDLE_MAX_AGE_MS"` across the repo. Read `worker/src/internal-ca-bundle.ts:17-35` (the only production consumer of the cached bundle — a bare `JSON.parse`, no verification). Read `worker/src/revocation.do.test.ts:197-292` for the fail-open bootstrap case. Read `worker/src/signing-authority.ts:88` for the refresh/max-age ordering.

## Fix

Documentation — a dated CORRECTION block in ADR-010, matching the format ADR-008 §299 already uses. The underlying wiring gap is tracked separately on the revocation bead.
acceptance_criteria: docs/design/010-cross-language-canonical-encoding.md carries a dated CORRECTION block on the Decision (2026-05-10) paragraph recording that isBundleStale/checkRevocation have no production caller, so the cited fail-closed behaviour is not exercised, and noting the fail-open-on-absent-bundle case. Original text retained (ADRs are append-only). `cd worker && npx vitest run` green.

title: Expose getEpochPublicKey on ReceiptSigner — cloister can only archive epochs it happened to observe
description:
Found 2026-08-04 answering "who publishes the Interlace epoch index?".

OWNERSHIP, since it was unclear: publication is CLOISTER's and already built. `/.well-known/interlace/index.json` is a declared route in their manifest (`wellKnownInterlace` kind), synthesized by `listActorCaBundleEpochs` from their `actor_ca_bundle` table, which already carries epoch, signing_key_pubkey_b64u, cert_der_b64u, issued_at_ms, retired_at_ms, status, compromise_notice_b64u and external_anchor_uri — the RECEIPTS.md §2.3 shape. Nothing to build there.

notme's half — retaining retired keys so they remain resolvable — landed in PR #64: the `retired_keys` table, written BEFORE the DELETE in rotate() (signing-authority.ts:1122 / :1130), plus getEpochPublicKey().

THE GAP: cloister populates its archive from what it OBSERVES, polling notme's /internal/ca-bundle (which publishes current + prev key only). If cloister misses an epoch — it wasn't running, or notme rotated twice between polls — that epoch is absent from cloister's archive permanently. notme HAS the key in retired_keys, but there is no way to hand it over: `ReceiptSigner` exposes only `receiptFacts` and `signReceipt`, pinned by rpc-surface.do.test.ts.

So the failure mode this bead closes is narrow but real: a receipt naming epoch N is unverifiable not because the key was destroyed (fixed) but because the only party publishing it never saw it.

FIX: expose it on the entrypoint —

    async epochPublicKey(epoch: number):
      Promise<{ ok: true; publicRawB64: string; kid: string; retiredAt: number | null }
             | { ok: false; code: "EPOCH_UNKNOWN"; message: string }>

Returning a union rather than null-or-throw, per ADR-016 rule 5. `EPOCH_UNKNOWN` must be honest: an auditor has to distinguish "notme does not have this" from a transport failure, and both currently look the same.

Then update rpc-surface.do.test.ts's ReceiptSigner allow-list — deliberately, in the same diff, because that test exists so a new RPC method cannot appear without someone deciding it should.

Nothing about this is public-facing on notme's side: it is a service-binding RPC, and the data is public key material already published in the CA bundle.

Related: notme-acd503 (the retention half, landed), notme-c1b7fd (receipt signing).
acceptance_criteria: `ReceiptSigner.epochPublicKey(epoch)` returns a result union resolving any epoch present in retired_keys or the current one, with EPOCH_UNKNOWN distinguishable from failure. rpc-surface.do.test.ts's allow-list updated in the same change. `task worker:check` green.

title: ADR-007 promises a kek-entropy-check that refuses a weak NOTME_KEK_SECRET; no such check exists — `NOTME_KEK_SECRET=weak` boots and seals the CA key
description:
Documentation-honesty audit finding (Goal Zero criterion A), notme-bed754. ADR-007 status is "Partially implemented (audited 2026-08-04)", but the 2026-08-04 audit note covers only the three "Problem" boundaries — it does not reach the adversarial-test table this finding is about.

## The claim

`docs/design/007-secretless-local-proxy.md`, §"Adversarial test strategy" → "Key extraction attacks" table:

| Test | Attack | Expected | Invariant |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kek-entropy-check` | Set `NOTME_KEK_SECRET=weak`, attempt startup | **Startup fails — secret too short** | #3 |

Invariant #3 in the same document is *"Fail closed on mode misconfiguration"*, and ARCHITECTURE.md:178 repeats it in the six "Secretless invariants (verified by adversarial tests)". The table's framing — a named test, an expected outcome, an invariant number — reads as shipped-and-verified.

## What is actually true

There is no minimum-length or entropy check on `NOTME_KEK_SECRET` anywhere, and no test named `kek-entropy-check`.

- `validateKeyStorageConfig` (`worker/src/platform.ts:73-85`) rejects exactly one condition: `mode === "encrypted" && !kekSecret`. A one-character secret passes.
- `deriveKek` (`worker/src/key-encryption.ts:75-81`) rejects `!secret` only. Its own comment explains why the empty case is fatal — *"every key would then be sealed under a value an attacker can guess in one try — strictly worse than plaintext, because it looks encrypted"* — which is the same argument that applies, with a slightly larger constant, to `weak`.
- `worker/src/__tests__/key-encryption.test.ts` has five tests; the closest is *"refuses an empty secret instead of deriving a guessable KEK"* (:73). `worker/src/__tests__/platform.test.ts:38-68` covers the four mode/secret combinations, passing `"ab".repeat(16)` as the valid secret — never a short one.
- `rg -i "weak|too short|entropy" worker/src/__tests__/*.ts worker/src/*.do.test.ts` returns no relevant hit.

So `NOTME_KEY_STORAGE=encrypted NOTME_KEK_SECRET=weak` starts cleanly and HKDF derives a usable KEK from four characters. HKDF stretches; it does not add entropy. The CA private key is then sealed under a secret in any wordlist, while the operator reads "encrypted at rest" and the audit note's headline claim — *"cat *.sqlite | strings | grep '\"d\"' … now holds whenever NOTME_KEK_SECRET is set"* — is technically true and practically hollow.

## Related, same file: the invariant cross-references in the tests are scrambled

Worth fixing in the same pass, because it breaks the doc→evidence trail ARCHITECTURE.md advertises. Against ADR-007's numbered list, five of six inline references in `worker/src/__tests__/adversarial.test.ts` point at the wrong invariant:

| test | says | ADR-007's actual number |
|---|---|---|
| `:13` header, `signing.key.isolation` | #4 | #2 (exportKey must throw) |
| `:23` non-extractable key rejects exportKey | #4 | #2 |
| `:160` rejects JWT with alg: none | #1 | not in the six at all |
| `:187` rejects expired token | #2 | not in the six at all |
| `:240`/`:243` bootstrap code single-use | #5 | not in the six (#5 is JTI replay) |
| `:299` error message leak | #6 | #4 |

## How verified

Read ADR-007 §"Security invariants" (:272-282) and §"Adversarial test strategy" (:286-320) in full. Read `worker/src/platform.ts:60-90` and `worker/src/key-encryption.ts:70-95`. Enumerated `key-encryption.test.ts` and `platform.test.ts` test names. `rg -n -i "too short|entropy|MIN_KEK" worker/src/key-encryption.ts worker/src/platform.ts` → no hits beyond the empty-secret guard. Compared ADR-007's numbered list against every `invariant #` reference via `rg -n "invariant #" worker/src/__tests__/*.ts worker/src/*.do.test.ts`.

## Fix

Both halves, and the code half is small and worth doing:

**Code** — add a minimum-length gate to `validateKeyStorageConfig` (and/or `deriveKek`, which is the true chokepoint since `signing-authority.ts:203` has its own fail-closed path) with the test ADR-007 already named. 32 bytes matches what `platform.test.ts` already treats as the canonical valid secret. Correct the six `invariant #N` comments in `adversarial.test.ts`.

**Documentation** — if a length gate is deliberately declined, the ADR row must say the check is unimplemented rather than describing its expected failure message. ADR-007's own audit-note format is the right vehicle.
acceptance_criteria: Either validateKeyStorageConfig/deriveKek rejects a NOTME_KEK_SECRET below a stated minimum length with a test named kek-entropy-check, or ADR-007's adversarial-test table marks that row unimplemented in a dated audit note. The six `invariant #N` comments in worker/src/__tests__/adversarial.test.ts match ADR-007 §"Security invariants" numbering. `cd worker && npx vitest run` green.

title: notme-proxy: UDS listen support (unix:/path/to/sock)
description:
Parent: rosary-ac0518.

The proxy's --listen flag already advertises 'unix:/run/notme/mtls.sock' in its docstring (proxy/src/main.rs:11) but the parser only handles SocketAddr (line 184). Implement the unix:PATH variant so cloister can route through notme-proxy via UDS without a TCP hop.

Implemented UDS listen support in proxy/src/main.rs (uncommitted on main):

comments.text:
Committed as 5bfcd63 on main.

**Security review additions over the initial draft:**
1. Socket file chmod'd to 0600 right after bind. The bridge cert means anyone with `connect()` access can fetch as the bridge identity — owner-only is the right default for the local-trust model from the parent epic. There's a microsecond chmod-after-bind race window; mitigated by directory perms (operator concern). A future hardening could set umask before bind for a tighter guarantee, but that needs a libc dep so it's out of scope here.
2. `try_remove_socket_file()` refuses to remove non-socket paths and uses `symlink_metadata` (not `metadata`) so a symlink at the path is treated as "not a socket" rather than followed. This protects against operator typos like `unix:./bridge-cert.pem` silently deleting the cert, and against an attacker placing a symlink at the target before startup.

**Validated 2x:**
- Pass 1: `cargo build` + `cargo test` (11/11) + `cargo clippy --tests -- -D warnings` — all clean
- Pass 2: `cargo clean` then `cargo test --release` (11/11) — all clean from a fresh build

**Test coverage (11 tests):**
- Parser: tcp / unix-absolute / unix-relative / empty-unix / invalid-tcp
- Stale removal: noop-when-absent / refuses-regular-file / refuses-symlink-to-regular-file
- Bind helper: sets 0600 perms / replaces stale socket / round-trip accept

Closing.

title: Chain-narrowing constraints are specified in ADR-008 and implemented nowhere — scope subsetting lives only inside a test
description:
ADR-008 specifies three constraints that make a delegated certificate chain safe. NONE of them exist in code. Verified 2026-08-06 at HEAD.

1. SCOPE SUBSETTING — ADR-008's verification pseudocode is explicit: `verify cert.scopes ⊆ parent.scopes // MUST check — not optional`. There is NO such check in production. The only implementation in the repo is `verifyScopeChain` at `worker/src/__tests__/adversarial.test.ts:648` — a one-line helper DEFINED INSIDE THE TEST FILE, exercised by six passing tests under the heading "adversarial: scope attenuation (008 — monotonic restriction)".

   So six green tests assert a real and important property OF A FUNCTION THAT EXISTS ONLY IN THE TEST. Nothing production does is touched by them. This is the purest instance yet of the pattern recorded on notme-bed754 — a green test proving a property of a path production never takes — and it is worse than an untested invariant, because the test suite actively reports the invariant as covered.

2. nameConstraints — ADR-008 §299 specifies it, including the exact syntax (`permittedSubtrees: URI:wimse://notme.bot/agent/*`) and the reason ("enforced by any conformant X.509 path validator, RFC 5280 §4.2.1.10, independent of the custom scope extension"). ZERO occurrences in code; the only hits in the repo are the ADR itself.

3. certificatePolicies / policyMappings — zero occurrences anywhere, ADR included. These are the standard mechanism for naming WHAT A TIER MEANS and for translating one authority's policy into another's during cross-certification, so their absence is the gap that blocks federation rather than depth.

── WHY THIS IS NOT EXPLOITABLE TODAY, AND WHY IT IS STILL P0 ──
No chain currently exists to validate. Every cert notme mints is CA=false (notme-600df1), so there is no intermediate and no parent/child pair for a subset rule to govern. The gap is LATENT, not live.

That is precisely what makes it urgent. The moment the orchestrator tier lands, delegation becomes possible and NOTHING constrains what a delegated cert may claim: not its scopes, not its namespace. A bridge could mint a task cert asserting scopes its parent never held, or an identity in a namespace belonging to another principal. The tests would stay green throughout, because they never touched production in the first place.

So this must land BEFORE or WITH hop 2, never after. Filed at P0 for sequencing, not for present exposure.

── WHAT THE FIX IS, and the design point behind it ──
The knob is not "how many tiers are allowed". Depth is not the risk; UNCONSTRAINED DELEGATION is. Every catastrophic PKI failure of this class — DigiNotar, TÜRKTRUST, ANSSI, Symantec — was an intermediate issuing for names it had no business issuing. That is a name-constraint failure, not a depth failure. N tiers with constraints at every level is safer than two tiers without them.

If each step must strictly narrow — scopes ⊆ parent AND names ⊆ parent — then depth BOUNDS ITSELF: a chain can only be as long as the namespace and scope set can be meaningfully subdivided. A monotone decreasing chain in a lattice terminates on its own. That is what macaroons and Biscuit formalise, and it is why neither needs a tier number.

Concretely:
- implement the subset check in production and DELETE the test-local helper, so the six existing tests bind to real code
- emit nameConstraints on any CA=true cert, per ADR-008 §299
- decide whether certificatePolicies is needed now (it is the federation lever, so it can wait until a second authority exists — but see the note below)

RELATED: notme-600df1 (the tier that would exercise all three), notme-77a024 (revocation unit), notme-9f84e6 (correlation — the same chain read downward). The federation question (two organisations each with their own authority) is recorded as a comment on notme-600df1 and is the reason certificatePolicies/policyMappings are named here rather than dismissed.

CORRECTION AFTER FORMAL REVIEW (theoretical-foundations-analyst, 2026-08-06). The CODE and TESTS are correct as committed; the THEORY stated in this bead and in scope-chain.ts's header was wrong, and wrong in a way that inverted the engineering conclusion.

── THE CLAIM THAT FAILED ──
I argued: "if each step must strictly narrow, depth bounds itself — a monotonically decreasing chain in a finite lattice terminates on its own, so no tier number is needed." False three times over:

1. `verifyScopeChain` accepts equality BY DESIGN (there is an explicit test, "child scopes = parent scopes — valid"). So the relation is REFLEXIVE, hence a preorder, hence NEVER well-founded. The constant chain S, S, S, … is an admissible infinite descent. The lattice does no bounding at all.
2. Even forbidding equality only bounds a chain at |S|+1 — with today's five scopes that is six tiers, and granting a root 100 scopes silently authorises 101. A depth limit set by whoever last added a scope string is not a formalisation.
3. The lattice is not staying finite. Once scopes are hierarchical — `sign:git` → `sign:git:repo` → … , which is where nameConstraints-style namespacing (§299) points — infinite STRICTLY decreasing chains exist too.

WORSE, MY CITATION PROVED THE OPPOSITE. Macaroons and Biscuit permit unbounded attenuation precisely BECAUSE authority cannot grow, and both then bound depth SEPARATELY and explicitly — Biscuit via block-count limits, macaroon deployments via caveat caps — because chain length is a verification-cost DoS vector even when authority is safe. Their lesson is "attenuation makes depth safe for AUTHORITY; depth still needs its own bound for RESOURCES."

── THE REPAIR, AND IT IS ALREADY IN THE DESIGN ──
Terminating a chain whose scopes may stay equal requires some OTHER component to strictly decrease: a rank function into a well-founded set. X.509 already carries it. RFC 5280 §6.1.4(l)/(m) is a LOOP VARIANT — `max_path_length` decremented at each non-self-issued intermediate and min'd with each cert's constraint. Chains terminate because ℕ has no infinite descent, not because P(S) is finite. SPKI/SDSI (RFC 2693) carries the degenerate case as a boolean delegation bit, and notme's two-hop design IS that boolean: bridge may delegate, task may not.

── THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES THIS A REAL ERROR RATHER THAN A PEDANTIC ONE ──
ADR-008 states the scope-subset check is COOPERATIVE enforcement — relying parties MUST perform it and nothing compels them to. `pathLenConstraint` is INTRINSIC: every conformant X.509 validator enforces it unasked. I argued the WEAKER cooperative mechanism made the STRONGER intrinsic one redundant. Exactly backwards. Two dimensions, two mechanisms, neither reducible to the other: this bead's subset rule is the AUTHORITY bound, `pathLenConstraint` is the DEPTH bound, and nameConstraints is the NAMESPACE bound.

── WHAT CHANGED IN CODE ──
Only the header comment of `worker/src/auth/scope-chain.ts`. `verifyScopeChain` keeps accepting equality — ⊆ is the correct SAFETY property (no escalation) and was never a termination property. Pass-through delegation must remain legal. No rank parameter added: the rank exists in the design as pathlen and is already pinned by delegation-depth.do.test.ts. 510 unit + 120 DO still passing.

── CONSEQUENCE FOR THE OPEN QUESTION ──
The answer to "is formalising the tier necessary?" flips from NO to YES — as a RELATIVE budget, never an absolute tier number (that half of the argument survived review; a cert sits at different absolute depths under different trust anchors, so an absolute number is not even well-defined per certificate). ADR-008's table at lines 274-280 ALREADY IS that formalisation. It is not missing; it is unimplemented. Which returns this to notme-600df1 unchanged in substance and better justified.

TWO CAVEATS ON pathlen worth carrying forward, both from the review: RFC 5280 §6.1.4(l) does NOT decrement for self-issued certificates, so pathlen bounds distinct ORGANISATIONAL tiers rather than literal chain length — the verification-cost bound does not follow from it. And §6.1.1 excludes the anchor's own certificate from path processing (applying anchor constraints is optional per RFC 5937), so a root's pathlen is enforced when it appears as an intermediate in a cross-certified path and typically ignored when it is the anchor.

CORRECTION — this bead's item 2 is WRONG, and so was ADR-008 §299 which it cited. Verified against RFC 5280 2026-08-06.

WHAT THIS BEAD CLAIMED: that `nameConstraints` is the NAMESPACE bound, specified in ADR-008 §299 with exact syntax (`permittedSubtrees: URI:wimse://notme.bot/agent/*`), enforced intrinsically by any conformant X.509 path validator, and merely unimplemented.

WHAT RFC 5280 §4.2.1.10 ACTUALLY SAYS: "For URIs, the constraint applies to the host part of the name. The constraint MUST be specified as a fully qualified domain name and MAY specify a host or a domain."

URI NAME CONSTRAINTS DO NOT CONSTRAIN PATHS. A constraint of `notme.bot` is satisfied by `wimse://notme.bot/anything`, so the `/agent/` segment is not scoped at all. A conformant validator does exactly the right thing, and it is not what ADR-008 assumed. So the mechanism is not "specified and unimplemented" — it is SPECIFIED AND NON-FUNCTIONAL, which is a different and worse state, because anyone reading §299 would have built against it and found nothing enforced.

THE ENFORCEMENT LABEL IN THIS BEAD WAS ALSO WRONG. It listed three bounds as authority=cooperative, depth=intrinsic, namespace=intrinsic. The namespace bound is NOT intrinsic by any available mechanism except one:

1. DISTINCT CONSTRAINED HOSTS (agents.notme.bot, workloads.notme.bot) — the ONLY intrinsically-enforced option, at the cost of putting kind back into the name, which is what ADR-019 D2 just took out of it.
2. An `otherName` with a registered OID, constrained via permittedSubtrees on that otherName type. Standards-shaped; blocked on notme-229dc3 (PEN) and its live arc collision with cloister.
3. A custom CRITICAL extension plus a validator that understands it. Criticality makes non-understanding verifiers REJECT rather than ignore, which is safe — but enforcement then lives in notme's verifier, not everyone's, so it is cooperative in the same sense the scope check is.

WHAT SURVIVES UNCHANGED, and it is most of the bead:
- The scope-subset finding stands and is FIXED (auth/scope-chain.ts, applied at certScopesForSession, six previously-orphaned tests now bound to production code).
- The depth finding stands: pathLenConstraint is intrinsic, the root advertises pathlen=1, no mint path produces an intermediate.
- The sequencing argument stands and is now STRONGER: the constraints must land with the middle tier, and one of them turns out not to exist at all rather than merely being unbuilt.

ADR-008 §299 has been corrected in place with a CORRECTION block (ADRs are append-only, and other documents cite it). ADR-019 D5 records the three options as an open question rather than a decision.

PATTERN NOTE for notme-bed754: this is the same shape as the others this cycle, one level up. The scope check was a real rule implemented only in a test. title: red-team:replay — receipt epoch is unresolvable after two rotations; A can repudiate every receipt it ever signed
description:
Filed from adversarial review of PR #61 (branch notme-c1b7fd-receipt-signing), protocol-replay/epoch-confusion lens.

## Location
- worker/src/signing-authority.ts:822 `rotate()`
- worker/src/signing-authority.ts:768 `generateBundle()`
- worker/src/signing-authority.ts:492 `getReceiptFacts()`
- Spec: cloister interlace-spec/0.2.0-draft/RECEIPTS.md §2.2.2 step 2, §2.3

## Captured message
Any signed Interlace receipt, i.e. `Ed25519_Sign(master_sk_N, commitment_cbor)` where the commitment names `epoch: N` and `actor_fp: SHA-256(pub_N)`.

## The defect
RECEIPTS.md §2.2.2 (V historical audit) requires the auditor to resolve the pubkey for the receipt's *named epoch* from an archival CA bundle, at arbitrary later time T. §2.3 makes this MUST: "Historical pubkeys remain resolvable by epoch number until A's CA bundle is decommissioned entirely... without that, A can defeat audits by aggressive key rotation."

notme cannot satisfy this today, and PR #61 does not add it:

1. `rotate()` executes `DELETE FROM keys WHERE id = 'authority'` — the epoch-N keypair is destroyed.
2. It then writes `prevKeyId` / `prevPubKey` into DO storage. Single slot, unconditionally overwritten on the next rotation. Depth = 1.
3. `generateBundle()` publishes `{ epoch, seqno, keys: {curKeyId: pub, prevKeyId: prevPub}, keyId, prevKeyId }`. `keys` is keyed by **keyId**, not by epoch. The bundle carries exactly one `epoch` field (the current one). There is no epoch → pubkey mapping for any historical epoch, and no `.well-known/interlace/index.json` exists in notme at all (the well-known routes are jwks.json, signet-authority.json, ca-bundle.pem, oauth-authorization-server, openid-configuration, security.txt).

Consequence: after the second `rotate()`, `pub_N` exists nowhere. Every receipt naming epoch N fails §2.2.2 step 2 permanently.

## Resulting state
A (notme+cloister) can void the evidentiary weight of every receipt it has ever issued with two administrative actions. §2.5 says a valid receipt plus absence of `nonce(r)` from D_A proves off-record admission. A receipt whose epoch pubkey cannot be resolved is not a valid receipt, so the §2.5 / §13.2 claim collapses to nothing. This is precisely the repudiation the receipt exists to prevent, and the adversary in a non-repudiation system *is* A.

The existing model actively fights this: worker/src/revocation.ts:55 defines `epoch_mismatch // token.epoch < bundle.epoch` as a *revocation reason*, and :364 rejects any keyId not equal to `bundle.keyId` or `bundle.prevKeyId`. notme's key lifecycle is built on "old epoch = dead", which is right for 10-minute access tokens and wrong for permanent evidence. PR #61 introduces the first artifact whose verifiability must outlive rotation, and reuses the token retention policy unchanged.

## Detection difficulty
A third-party auditor cannot distinguish "A rotated twice and lost the key" from "this receipt was forged" from "A is stonewalling". Both present as an unresolvable epoch. Silence is not evidence here — it is indistinguishable from data loss, which §2.3's lost-bundle-recovery section explicitly tries to close via `external_anchor_uri`.

## Closing playbook
1. Add a `retired_keys(epoch INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, key_id TEXT, public_raw_b64 TEXT, retired_at INTEGER)` table; `rotate()` inserts the outgoing (epoch, keyId, pubkey) *before* the DELETE. Never prune.
2. Serve `/.well-known/interlace/index.json` per §2.3: every epoch entry with `status: "active" | "retired"`, retirement timestamp, and a published `ca_decommission_after`.
3. Key the receipt-verification lookup by **epoch**, not keyId. The bundle's `keys` map cannot answer "pubkey for epoch N".
4. §2.3(1): publish each per-epoch pubkey to an independent append-only anchor at mint time (`external_anchor_uri`) so a notme data-loss event does not silently look like a successful repudiation.
5. ADR-014 should state the retention obligation explicitly — it currently mentions retired epochs only at line 112, as a reason to derive `epoch`, and says nothing about keeping the key resolvable.

## Severity
BLOCKER / HIGH. Confidence 8/10 on the mechanism (verified in code); the adversary is the operator, which is the correct threat model for non-repudiation.
acceptance_criteria: A test in worker/src/signing-authority.do.test.ts that rotates twice and then resolves the pubkey for the original epoch from the published bundle/well-known surface, and succeeds. Run: `cd worker && pnpm vitest run src/signing-authority.do.test.ts`.

title: red-team:replay — timestamp_ms is unbounded, letting a compromised binding holder backdate fabricated receipts arbitrarily
description:
Filed from adversarial review of PR #61 (branch notme-c1b7fd-receipt-signing), protocol-replay/evidence-forgery lens.

## Location
worker/src/receipts/commitment.ts:193 — `const timestampMs = requireUint(decoded, "timestamp_ms");` and nothing else. Any non-negative safe integer is accepted (0 .. 9_007_199_254_740_991 ms, i.e. 1970 .. year 287396).

## Captured message / attacker position
Anything holding the `ReceiptSigner` service binding: a compromised cloister deployment, a compromised Worker in the same account, or a supply-chain compromise of cloister's build.

## Why this is in-scope rather than "the design trusts the binding holder"
ADR-014's own premise is that cloister holding `RECEIPT_SIGNING_KEY` in its env is unsafe and the key belongs in notme. If the binding holder were trusted absolutely, moving the key buys nothing. The PR clearly agrees — it bounds the compromise on several axes:
- cross-format forgery: blocked (parse + canonical re-encode + byte equality)
- `actor_fp`: derived, not received
- `epoch`: derived, not received
- `status`: pinned to 2xx, with the explicit stated reason "Signing one for a 4xx/5xx would let a caller manufacture evidence that a request it never served succeeded" (commitment.ts:186-188)

`timestamp_ms` is the one remaining field that is (a) fully attacker-chosen, (b) semantically load-bearing, and (c) cheaply boundable by notme — and it is unbounded. `nonce`, `request_hash`, `body_hash`, `headers_hash` are correctly left unvalidated because notme structurally cannot see the request; `timestamp_ms` has no such excuse, notme has a clock.

## Concrete exploit
A compromised binding holder mints N receipts with attacker-chosen `nonce`, `request_hash`, `body_hash`, `headers_hash`, `status: 200`, and `timestamp_ms` spread across the last two years. Each is a valid Ed25519 signature under A's master key over a canonical commitment. Under §2.5, each one whose nonce is absent from D_A is proof that A admitted a request off-record. A cannot disprove any of them — the signature is A's own.

The spec's live clock check does not help. §2.2.1 step 12 bounds `timestamp_ms` to ±300s of **P's** clock, and §2.2.2 audit reuses that step. The attacker is the party supplying both the receipt and the claimed request, so it simply asserts a matching request time. Only notme-side clamping constrains the value.

With clamping, the same compromise yields receipts that can only be dated to the window in which the attacker actually held the binding — bounded, correlatable with notme's own access records, and impossible to backfill into a fabricated history.

## Detection difficulty
An offline auditor holding the master pubkey sees a perfectly valid receipt. There is nothing in the signed bytes that distinguishes a backdated fabrication from a genuine two-year-old admission.

## Closing playbook
In `validateCommitment`, after `requireUint`:

```
const now = Date.now();
if (timestampMs < now - RECEIPT_CLOCK_SKEW_MS || timestampMs > now + RECEIPT_CLOCK_SKEW_MS) {
  fail("TIMESTAMP_OUT_OF_WINDOW", ...);
}
```

Pass `nowMs` in via `CommitmentFacts` (alongside `actorFp` / `epoch`) so it stays derived-not-received and remains testable. 300_000 ms matches RECEIPTS.md §2.2.1 step 12 and 0.1.0 §6.2.7, so the clamp is spec-justified and cannot reject a receipt a conformant P would have accepted. Both notme and cloister run on Cloudflare's clock, so real skew is sub-second.

Also document the residual in ADR-014: even clamped, a compromised binding holder can fabricate `nonce` / `request_hash` / `body_hash` / `headers_hash` freely. That is structurally unboundable and should be stated, not left implicit.

## Severity
MEDIUM. Confidence 8/10.
acceptance_criteria: Tests in worker/src/__tests__/receipt-commitment.test.ts assert rejection of a commitment with timestamp_ms far in the past (e.g. 0) and far in the future, and acceptance within the tolerance window. Run: `cd worker && pnpm vitest run src/__tests__/receipt-commitment.test.ts`.

title: First-boot bootstrap is hostile: an unauthenticated stranger's first request mints the admin code into the logs
description:
The first-boot experience is both bad ergonomics and a poor security posture, and the notme-976385 regeneration fix — correct on its own terms — made the second half sharper.

WHAT HAPPENS NOW. A fresh authority has no admin. The FIRST unauthenticated POST to /auth/passkey/register/options (worker.ts:833) causes getOrCreateBootstrapCode() to mint a code, console.log it, and return 401 "bootstrap code required — check Worker logs (wrangler tail)". The deployer is expected to go read Worker logs, find a UUID, and resubmit with it.

WHY IT IS BAD:
- THE TRIGGER IS NOT THE DEPLOYER. Any stranger who hits the endpoint first causes the mint. The code goes to the logs regardless of who asked, so an attacker chooses the moment a credential appears — and since notme-976385 made regeneration possible while no authenticator exists, they can cause it repeatedly. The security review judged this acceptable because the code never crosses the HTTP boundary (the caller gets a 401 with no code), so a network-only attacker gains nothing; the exposure is to anyone who can read Workers Logs, and invocation_logs = true persists them. That reasoning holds, and it is still a side channel as the primary onboarding path.
- SECRETS VIA LOG-SCRAPING is the exact posture this repo exists to eliminate everywhere else. notme's whole thesis is no long-lived secret on disk, OIDC/attestation instead of stored credentials — and then first boot says "go read a secret out of the logs".
- THE MESSAGE CAN BE A LIE. getOrCreateBootstrapCode returns null when an authenticator already exists, but worker.ts:833 DISCARDS the return value and emits the same "check Worker logs" 401 unconditionally. In the null case nothing was logged, so the operator is told to look for something that is not there (also noted by the type-correctness review).

THE DESIGN ALREADY HAS A BETTER ANSWER, and it is the intended flow: GitHub OIDC attestation bootstraps you once (/cert/gha verifies a real RS256 JWT against GitHub's JWKS and checks the owner allowlist), you generate a passkey locally, the bridge cert ties it to that login, and from then on you mint ephemeral certs yourself. That path needs no log-scraping and no shared secret, and it is ALREADY WIRED for GitHub. The log code is effectively the fallback for a deployer with no OIDC identity — self-hosters, air-gapped installs — rather than the primary path it currently is.

DIRECTION TO DECIDE: make attestation-based bootstrap the documented and default first-boot path; keep a non-OIDC fallback for self-hosters but make it an explicit operator action (a wrangler command, a one-shot admin invite) rather than something a stranger's HTTP request triggers; and fix the unconditional 401 message so it distinguishes "a code was minted, go look" from "this authority already has an administrator".

RELATED: notme-2c4209 (registration policy, blocked on notme-600df1) — whatever bootstrap becomes must be consistent with whether registration is open. notme-77438b (SPIFFE inversion) — the OIDC-bootstraps-passkey chain is the human-bootstraps-machine evidence.

PARTIALLY FIXED — the two mechanical halves are done (commits 1ebbf7e, 079b1f1). The DESIGN half, which is what this bead is really about, is still open.

DONE — the misleading 401. getOrCreateBootstrapCode returned string|null and worker.ts called it for its SIDE EFFECT, then answered "bootstrap code required — check Worker logs" unconditionally. In the closed case nothing is logged, so an operator was sent hunting a UUID that does not exist. The return type is now a discriminated state ({status:"issued",code} | {status:"closed"}), which is the actual fix — a caller cannot discard it, and the type checker found all eight call sites. The route now answers "this authority already has an administrator — sign in with a passkey, or ask an admin for an invite" when closed.

DONE, AND MORE SUBSTANTIVE — found while doing the above, in two stages, which is worth recording because the first attempt was a half-fix:
(a) #hasAuthenticator gated only the CONSUMED branch, so an UNUSED code minted before the first admin stayed returnable afterwards.
(b) Fixing (a) still left CONSUMPTION ungated. A code minted while nobody could authenticate, captured from the logs and never redeemed, remained REDEEMABLE after an administrator existed — and POST /cert consumes bootstrap codes to mint authorityManage+certMint. Mint-side gating cannot cover this: the code was legitimately issued when it was valid; only the consumer knows the authority has since gained a way in. The invariant is now stated once and enforced at BOTH ends: a bootstrap code is valid ONLY while nobody can authenticate. Regression tests cover both the refusal and the recovery case the guard exists to serve.

What changed is that the code is now useless once an admin exists, and the error message no longer lies.

comments.text:
A READY-MADE ANSWER FOR THE SELF-HOSTER BOOTSTRAP — from gitsign v0.17.0 (2026-07-29), which added an OAuth DEVICE-CODE flow with a configurable URL opener for interactive OIDC login.

THE GAP THIS ADDRESSES. The direction recorded on this bead is: make attestation-based bootstrap the default (GitHub OIDC → bridge cert → local passkey, already wired), and demote the log-scraped code to an explicit fallback for deployers with no OIDC identity. But "no OIDC identity" was doing a lot of work in that sentence, and the fallback it justified is the log-scraping this bead exists to remove.

The real constraint for a self-hoster running the local workerd container is not that they lack an OIDC identity — most have GitHub, Google, or an enterprise IdP. It is that the authorization-code redirect flow assumes a BROWSER ON THE SAME MACHINE with a reachable redirect URI. A container on a headless box, an air-gapped-ish host, or a terminal session has no such thing. So the design fell back to a shared secret in the logs.

DEVICE CODE (RFC 8628) IS THE STANDARD SOLUTION TO EXACTLY THAT SHAPE: the device shows a code, the human authenticates on a phone or laptop they already have, and the device polls until authorized. No redirect URI, no browser on the host, no shared secret transiting the logs, and the human-presence property this authority wants is preserved — better than a log-scraped code, since it authenticates a PERSON rather than proving log access.

WHY IT IS WORTH TAKING SERIOUSLY RATHER THAN NOTING: gitsign adopting it means the pattern is now normal in the Sigstore-adjacent tooling this ecosystem already uses, so a notme deployer would recognise the flow instead of learning a bespoke one. It also composes with the existing design rather than replacing it — the bootstrap still ends in a bridge cert and a local passkey; only the "how does the human prove who they are on a headless host" step changes.

NOT PROPOSING IT AS DECIDED. This bead's direction still needs the call recorded, and device code has real costs: notme would need an OIDC client registration per provider, a polling endpoint, and a decision about which IdPs are acceptable — which is entangled with notme-2c4209 (registration policy) and notme-600df1 (what the authority names). Filing it here so the fallback question is not answered as "keep the log code" by default, when a standard, better-understood option exists.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
THIRD MECHANICAL FIX IN THIS AREA (commit 538eead) — registration challenges now expire on the same clock as authentication challenges.

The two sibling lookups in auth/passkey.ts disagreed: authentication filtered `created_at > datetime('now','-5 minutes')`, registration selected on `user_id` alone. So a registration challenge stayed valid until the one-hour sweep, a twelve-fold longer replay window, and with no ORDER BY the row chosen among several was arbitrary — a stale challenge could win over the fresh one the caller had just requested. Both are fixed.

Not remotely exploitable on its own (the challenge is a fresh unguessable server value), which is precisely why it survived: it is an unintended asymmetry between two functions that should agree, not a decision anyone made. Those stop being harmless the moment something else leaks.

RUNNING TALLY OF WHAT IS NOW DONE IN THIS AREA, so the remaining scope is unambiguous:
- The 401 no longer lies — the return type is a discriminated state, so the caller cannot emit "check Worker logs" when nothing was logged.
- The bootstrap invariant is enforced at BOTH mint and consume — a code minted pre-admin is no longer redeemable after an authenticator exists.
- Registration challenge freshness and ordering (this commit).

WHAT REMAINS IS THE DESIGN DECISION, unchanged and not something more code fixes: a stranger's first unauthenticated request still causes a bootstrap code to be minted into the Worker logs on a fresh authority, and log-scraping is still the documented onboarding path for a self-hoster.

The two candidate answers are both on record now — attestation-first (GitHub OIDC → bridge cert → local passkey, already wired for GitHub) as the default, with the fallback for deployers who cannot use it being either an explicit operator action or the RFC 8628 device-code flow that gitsign adopted. The device-code option is the one worth weighing seriously, because the actual constraint was never "the deployer has no OIDC identity" but "the redirect flow assumes a browser on the same host", and device code solves exactly that while authenticating a PERSON rather than proving log access.

That decision is entangled with notme-2c4209 (registration policy) and notme-600df1 (what the authority names), and should be made with them rather than ahead of them.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
THE PRIMARY DEFECT IS FIXED AND DEPLOYED — production commit 2f0b1598, converged, worker:verify 14/14.

WHAT CHANGED. The public registration route called `getOrCreateBootstrapCode()`, so the first UNAUTHENTICATED request to a fresh authority MINTED an admin bootstrap code and console.logged it. The trigger was never the deployer: any stranger could cause the mint, and since notme-976385 made regeneration possible while no authenticator exists, could cause it repeatedly — choosing the moment a credential appeared in the log.

Now the route performs a READ. `getBootstrapState()` returns one of `closed` / `armed` / `unconfigured`, carries no code in any variant, and mints nothing. The property that matters is that the answer is STABLE UNDER REPETITION — pinned by a test — because that is what removes the attacker's ability to drive credential creation on demand.

MINTING MOVED BEHIND AN OPERATOR ACTION: `wrangler secret put BOOTSTRAP_CODE`. Setting it requires control of the DEPLOYMENT, where the mechanism it replaces required only the ability to send an HTTP request and read a log. Declared as a SECRET rather than a var deliberately — it grants `authorityManage`, and vars are readable from the dashboard and echoed in deploy output. Minimum 16 chars, trimmed, so an empty or whitespace `secret put` cannot arm an authority with a value a caller could guess by sending nothing.

Consume prefers the operator secret, compared timing-safe (it grants authorityManage, so a comparison leaking position would let a caller recover it byte by byte), and FALLS THROUGH to the legacy stored code rather than returning early — an authority armed before this change is not stranded.

THE LOG-SCRAPING JUSTIFICATION IS NOW EMPIRICALLY DEAD, not just philosophically wrong. This cycle proved `wrangler tail` returns nothing for a failing request AND for a known-good 200 issued in the same window, in production. So the documented recovery path could simply fail to work — the operator is told to read something they may be unable to read. The new messages never mention logs, and a test asserts the absence of /log/i as well as the presence of the new instruction, because a message naming both paths would send operators hunting for a credential that was never created.

TWO GUARDS FIRED AND BOTH WERE RIGHT:
- The 401-message test pinned the old "check Worker logs" wording. Updated to the new contract.
- The RPC surface pin moved 42 → 43, with the review recorded inline: `getBootstrapState` is STRICTLY SAFER than what it displaces. It returns one of three words; the method it removes from the unauthenticated path mints an admin credential as a side effect of being called. A leaked stub learns only whether an authority has an administrator, which /auth/passkey/status already answers publicly.

STILL OPEN, and the reason this bead does not close: the audit's second recommendation was to make ATTESTATION-BASED BOOTSTRAP THE DOCUMENTED DEFAULT first-boot path — /cert/gha already verifies a real RS256 JWT against GitHub's JWKS and checks the owner allowlist, so it needs no shared secret at all. That path exists and works; what is missing is the documentation making it the primary route, with BOOTSTRAP_CODE positioned as the fallback for self-hosters and air-gapped installs. The error message for `unconfigured` already names both.

Production is unaffected by any of this — it has an administrator, so bootstrap is `closed` there. The change matters for fresh deploys: staging, self-hosters, and anyone standing up a new authority.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

acceptance_criteria: First boot has a documented default path that does not require reading a secret out of logs and cannot be triggered by an unauthenticated stranger; any retained fallback is an explicit operator action; and the register/options 401 distinguishes "code minted" from "authority already has an administrator" rather than emitting one message unconditionally.

title: cert-authority.ts + signing-authority.ts + token.ts — Ed25519 as any casts are a WebCrypto TS lib gap, document it
description:
Multiple security-critical crypto call sites use `{ name: "Ed25519" } as any` or `"Ed25519" as any` to work around a missing Ed25519 entry in the TypeScript DOM lib's `SubtleCrypto` overloads:

- `worker/src/cert-authority.ts`: lines 48, 65, 115
- `worker/src/signing-authority.ts`: lines 126, 136, 155, 192, 279, 311, 423
- `worker/src/auth/token.ts`: lines 78, 113

These `as any` casts suppress type-checking on the algorithm parameter passed to `crypto.subtle.generateKey/importKey/sign/verify`. If the string is wrong (e.g., typo or wrong casing), the runtime throws but TS doesn't catch it at compile time.

The casts are structurally necessary given the current `@cloudflare/workers-types` lib — Ed25519 was added to the spec but typings lag. However they are undocumented, making them look like lazy workarounds.

Fix options:
1. Add a top-of-file comment in each affected file explaining the cast is a DOM lib gap, not a type escape hatch. (docs)
2. Define a typed `const ED25519_ALGO = { name: "Ed25519" } as AlgorithmIdentifier` constant and use it throughout — narrows the surface of `as any` to one declaration. (tidy)

The `cert-exchange.ts:142` cast `(body.proof as any).type` in the exhaustive-check branch is a TypeScript narrowing artifact — correct but worth a comment.
The `auth/principals.ts:106,176` `.toArray() as any[]` casts hide SQLite row shapes — these are medium risk as they bypass row type checking on security-relevant principal lookups.

Severity: medium for Ed25519 casts (documented gap, low bug risk), medium for principals.ts (hides shape mismatches on security queries).
Action: docs + tidy
Labels: perspective:dev, action:docs, action:tidy

comments.text: Test comment — checking MCP write path after schema migration.

- worker/src/auth/token.ts (2 sites)
- worker/src/signing-authority.ts (2 sites)
- worker/src/cert-exchange.ts (1 site)

SECURITY.md gained an "Ed25519 typing workaround" section under "Known Limitations" explaining the gap, the convention, and what changes when the lib types catch up.

Tests retain their own inline casts because they construct distinct algorithm-object shapes per call (importKey wants the object form, sign accepts the string form) — that's documented in the platform.ts header so future contributors don't get confused.

title: notme: M1 — OIDC audience pin "notme.bot" incoherent for Google ID tokens
description:
Found by code-review sub-agent (aa0878f69907df240).

Multiple OIDC-accepting routes pin `expectedAudience: "notme.bot"`:
- worker/worker.ts:1307 (/connections POST)
- worker/worker.ts:1422 (/join)
- worker/worker.ts:1465 (/auth/oidc/login)
- worker/src/cert-exchange.ts:106

But Google ID tokens carry `aud = <google-client-id>.apps.googleusercontent.com`, never `notme.bot`. So either:
(a) These OIDC paths cannot accept Google tokens at all today (audience check always fails),
(b) The audience pin is wrong and should be the Google client ID from env, OR
(c) The OIDC paths are dead code that should be removed.

`TRUSTED_ISSUERS` in verify-proof.ts:43 includes `https://accounts.google.com`, suggesting (a)/(c) — Google was meant to work.

The synthetic test at gen/ts/__tests__/dpop-verifier.test.ts uses `iss: https://accounts.google.com` + `aud: notme.bot` — a configuration that can't exist in practice.

**First-principles options:**
1. Remove the Google branch from TRUSTED_ISSUERS until the audience plumbing is right
2. Add per-issuer audience expectations: `Map<issuer, expected-audience>` keyed by env config (e.g. `OIDC_CLIENT_ID_GOOGLE`)
3. Drop the OIDC paths entirely if they're not used

The structural fix landed in 5639328 (audience required at type level) is correct — this is just about the VALUE being pinned looking wrong for some issuers.

title: notme: M2 — passkey_challenges grows unbounded (no sweeper)
description:
Found by code-review sub-agent.

worker/src/auth/passkey.ts:248 — the new lookup `WHERE challenge = ? AND created_at > datetime('now', '-5 minutes')` filters expired rows at READ time but never deletes them.

The 0c5e296 fix (challenge per-flow binding) made each row keyed by its random challenge value. Successful flows DELETE their row at line 277-280. Abandoned flows (user closes browser, network failure) leave dead rows forever.

Fix options:

3. Use a TTL-aware storage (e.g. KV with expirationTtl) instead of SQLite

Option 2 is simplest and bounds growth at the rate of new auth attempts.
